utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on channel 4, where I usually get the English translation. Since it seems that we -- that the technical problem has been solved, I'd rather start again and ask again, Madam Registrar, to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Loukas, you were on your feet. But before I give you an opportunity address the Chamber, I'd first like to turn into private session for a short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Just in relation to the order of the next witnesses, I would -- as Your Honour is aware, I'm currently in the middle of my cross-examination of Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I understand that the next witness is KRAJ 461, a witness for whom heretofore there was a question of whether or not he would be seeking protective measures. The situation is there that I received some additional material in relation to that witness after court yesterday, and some additional material in relation to that witness the day before, which included a transcript of his previous evidence, from Mr. Harmon. Now, I realised last night, when I was going through the transcript of that particular witness, that I hadn't received the cross-examination of that witness -- at the end of the evidence in chief and the cross-examination, because it went on the next day, and I only had one day's worth of transcript. So I've had an opportunity, as Mr. Harmon kindly provided me with that additional transcript just prior to court this morning, I've had an opportunity to skim through that transcript. I don't think my cross-examination of that particular witness will be very long, but I'd like the opportunity to read the rest of the transcript prior to cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So in terms of the order in relation to the following witness, who I also understand is in all likelihood seeking protective measures, 039, I'm just wondering if we could, once the evidence in chief of that first witness is completed, if the evidence in chief of the second witness could be completed while I have an opportunity to review the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Tieger, any objection against the proposal of Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I can begin with just a quick clarification of the record, and not in the spirit of finger pointing but just to make the record clear. Those were not additional materials disclosed, those were materials re-disclosed. Those materials were originally disclosed in April 2003. I might also note that they are available on the Internet. Nevertheless, it is correct, as I understand it, that the re-disclosed materials did not include the portion to which Ms. Loukas referred. She does have those this morning. Now, with that clarification, to directly address the Court's question: I understand that the second witness was required to review materials from previous testimony, and it is -- he would have been available pursuant to the earlier schedule, which would have had him taking the stand in the afternoon. Of course, he is -- he will be ready to proceed at that time. Based on this new proposal, I am not in a position to say he could proceed immediately after the direct of the next scheduled witness. So that -- there would be a logistical issue involved that may or may not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- require an interlude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take whatever measures which would facilitate examination-in-chief immediately following. I do understand that it was only foreseen that it would be this afternoon, but if you could try to make him available at the earliest moment possible. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just -- I'd like to make a clarification upon Mr. Tieger's clarification. I would indicate on this question of the transcript being available on the Internet, the situation is that there were portions that were in fact redacted and were not available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- on the Internet. So I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- if there's any -- I can imagine that these points arise. I'd rather now proceed, and we have a very tight schedule.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this does not add to what we have on our mind at this moment, that is, to finish with the witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But of course the Chamber is quite willing to listen to these kind of smaller adjustments once we are back from our week off. So it's not to say that we are not interested to hear it, but perhaps this is the moment where we should --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just one second point, if I might make it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Also in relation to what Mr. Tieger just said. I would indicate that it wasn't the case that that particular witness, the second witness, would in fact start in the afternoon even on the schedule previously anticipated, because the idea was that there would be one hour in relation to the rest of my cross-examination, one hour and a quarter in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask Mr. Tieger to look at it that he could be here as soon as possible, and if he's not here, we'll certainly consider whose fault it is to the extent that it helps us. But I do understand that you disagree with the scheduling as presented by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Then I think -- you are ready to continue the cross-examination of Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Hasanovic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hasanovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Ms. Loukas will now continue the cross-examination. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, you'll recall that when we adjourned for the day yesterday, I was asking you about your awareness of various background events. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, were you aware that, on or around the 9th of May, 1992, that Serbs from Srebrenica left there and came to Bratunac? That's Serb civilians. And on the same day, Muslims from Bratunac left and moved to Srebrenica. Were you aware of those particular movements of people?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot hear very well in my earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: Test. Test.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You now better hear, Mr. Hasanovic, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So I take it, Mr. Hasanovic, you didn't hear the last question because of the technical difficulties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hasanovic, you'll recall that when we left off yesterday, I was asking you some background questions in relation to Bratunac. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I just want to ask you if you were aware that on or around the 9th of May, 1992, that Serb civilians from Srebrenica left that particular town and came to Bratunac, and on the same day, Muslims from Bratunac left Bratunac and went to Srebrenica. Were you aware of those movements of people?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of such movements in those directions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Were you aware that Naser Oric had become commander of the Muslim armed forces in that area?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, of course, prior to your coming to give evidence in court yesterday, of course you had a proofing session on the 18th of April with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in relation to that proofing session, I think you indicated to the Court that it took a period of -- if you might remind the Court how long.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It took one day; several hours the first day, and an hour the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: This is your proofing with the Prosecution just prior to giving evidence yesterday you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So approximately how many hours was that?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Altogether, it lasted four to five hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, one of the matters that you indicated in your proofing session was this, and I'd like to confirm it with you. And I'll read it out slowly for the benefit of the interpreters, and of course for your benefit, Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We do have a B/C/S copy of the proofing notes that may assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If, Ms. Loukas would like to use them, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I didn't propose to go through the entire proofing note, which covers some five pages. It was just a particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are available in B/C/S in case the witness would need to consult them and if that would be a logical consequence of your questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Perhaps if the B/C/S copy might be made available for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, I think you've got the B/C/S copy of your proofing notes in front of you.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, if you go to paragraph 3 of your five-page proofing note, you'll see that what you have stated there was that: "Later, when we were detained in the Vuk Karadzic school, the Serbs said that they were fighting against these paramilitaries but they were not successful. Other people thought that everything would be in order once the paramilitaries were out of the region. The Serb guards stated that everything would be in order as soon as the Serb leadership is able to throw out those who were paid by -- they did not know whom, and were ordered to come by they did not know whom." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So that was a matter that you covered in your proofing session with the Prosecution, and of course that is indeed correct, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm that with you, Mr. Hasanovic, as it was a matter that was not elicited in your evidence in chief. Now, the other matter, Mr. Hasanovic, is this: In your statement of the 7th of April of the year 2000, at page 5 --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And again, it might be suitable to give Mr. Hasanovic access to the B/C/S copy of his statement prior to my asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you have that before you now, Mr. Hasanovic. If you'd like to turn to paragraph 24. Have you got that before you, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you'll note there that you mention: "The day after the police department split, the Serbs were wearing their own Serbian uniforms with Serbian state insignias." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Could you describe the uniform for me.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the police was divided, the Serbs kept the same uniforms. However, new people were recruited to the police from the ranks of civilians and they used the same uniforms, with the only difference being that on their sleeves there were the insignia of the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And how big was that?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were insignia worn either on sleeves or on the blouse pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'll again ask my question: How big was it?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that. The size was three centimetres by two centimetres, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it depicted the flag of the Serbian Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere? Could you indicate with your hands what the size approximately was, so that we can get a better impression.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was approximately the size, and these were the dimensions of that emblem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what the witness indicates, it's far more than two by three centimetres, Ms. Loukas. The Chamber notes that it was anything between 7 and 10 centimetres, rather than 2 by 3 centimetres. And since I had some difficulty in understanding such a small insignia, I asked the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And where was this insignia?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one of the sleeves of the police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Where on the sleeve?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the left sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: What colour was it?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was blue and white. There was another colour that I can't remember at this moment. And I believe that there was the inscription of the Serbian Krajina, the so-called Birac, denoting all of the Serbian municipalities that they proclaimed in that region.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, moving on to another topic. If you turn the page, and that is at page 6, have you got paragraph 31 in front of you? Do you see that paragraph, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see paragraph 31. However, it is on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's on page 4 in the B/C/S version, is it?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 31, you indicate this: "The Territorial Defence unit never had any weapons. My brother and the others had tried to obtain some, but we were never successful. We managed to get a few hunting rifles from families but never any substantial weapons." Do you see that portion there, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. From whom did your brother and the others try to obtain some weapons?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to obtain weapons in order to create a team. This team, in case of attack, would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you? Could you please carefully listen to the question. The question was: From whom you sought to obtain weapons. Not the purpose for which you wanted to have these weapons, but from whom. Could you carefully listen to the question and try to answer that question specifically. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We tried to contact the Muslim authorities in Bratunac in order to obtain weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And who were the Muslim authorities in Bratunac that you tried to obtain these weapons from?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were representatives of the SDA, one of whom was the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And who was that, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nijaz Durakovic was the president, and the president of the SDA was Mr. Dzevad Gusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And what was your purpose in trying to obtain these weapons?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Why were you trying to obtain the weapons, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally tried to obtain weapons because of the atmosphere. Terrible things were happening all around us. We believed that we should have weapons in order to be able to defend ourselves in case of attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: When did you try and obtain the weapons?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was when the conflict escalated in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So around what date are you talking about, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that. It was sometime at the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: When you say the conflict in Croatia escalated, of course, the conflict in Croatia commenced in 1991, so what do you mean by the escalation?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that we couldn't see an end to that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So there was a fear amongst the people in your community that the conflict nearby in Croatia may spill over to where you were?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, how many people in your area of Suha had weapons?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. There were some hunting rifles that individuals had. I don't know who had them, because people who had them did not dare show it. They didn't dare say that they had them.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But in any event, through your position in the SDA, you were aware that people had weapons, that Muslims had weapons.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position in the SDA was very weak. I worked in the morning every day. I did not attend any sessions of the party. I know that some people got weapons from the police station in Bratunac. Those weapons were distributed equally amongst the Serbs and the Muslims, and those people kept those weapons at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: When did that distribution occur, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this happened in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And as you've indicated, to both Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what was the total number of the distribution of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, just going back to the evidence you were giving yesterday. You were describing the events of the 10th of May, and I think you indicated that you said to your wife that you had to lie low, and you went and hid in some bushes. You recall that evidence yesterday, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you described -- you joined your family at a later point. You found your wife and children, and together with them, you started walking towards the town. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by the Prosecution: Can you describe the soldiers that were walking with the people, and you said that the soldiers mostly wore the uniforms of the Yugoslav army. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you said "mostly our neighbours from Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: What did the uniform actually look like, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore summer military uniforms, and most probably it belonged to the military department, in the depot of the military department in Bratunac and was kept there as the reserve uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, I take it you at some stage completed your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the situation is, when you complete your military service, that once you've completed that and you register that you've finished, that you're then registered as a reserve. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. According to military rules, all those who completed compulsory military service were members of the reserve in case of war. However, I personally was never invited to attend any additional training or manoeuvres or any such thing after the compulsory service that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. According to the military rules, all those who complete their compulsory military service are members of the reserve. So you agree with that proposition? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And when you're in the -- when one was in the reserves at that point, of course, one has a uniform and boots and what have you. You'd agree with that proposition, wouldn't you, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to this evidence you gave yesterday. At one point you also indicated that when you were coming close to the stadium, you noticed a car, you recognised the car, you saw two soldiers come out of the car, and one of them was Krke. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krke had a black uniform on, and the other two soldiers wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And when you say "military," can you describe what you mean by "military."

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the military uniform worn by the reserve or the uniform worn by the former Yugoslav army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, further in relation to the evidence you gave yesterday in relation to Branko Jovanovic, the man who hurt you personally, you gave evidence. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you said that he was wearing a military uniform. Can you describe that military uniform?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It is the same uniform that I've already described. Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally believe that this uniform belonged to all the citizens of the former Yugoslavia, including the army, up to the moment when the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina organised the referendum on independence and secession from the rest of Yugoslavia. This is what was done. I personally attended the referendum, and the vast majority of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina decided to -- that they wanted to live in an independent state. This is what was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Do I understand that when you're describing these uniforms, you say they were the uniforms everyone would have up to the referendum in which the people voted on independence? Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. My opinion is that it belonged to us and that all of us citizens recognised it as the uniform of our own army up to the moment when the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina stopped being an integral part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, just in relation to these -- now, Mr. Hasanovic, just in relation to these uniforms, I was asking you some questions earlier about the reserves. Now, of course, everybody who was in the reserves had a uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had uniforms, but these uniforms were kept in a depot in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, the situation is, Mr. Hasanovic, that people were often allowed to keep their uniforms at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, this is not a question but you say what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "Mr. Hasanovic, the situation is..." It's not a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, it's an assertion, to which I'm inviting his agreement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas asked you whether the people were often allowed to keep their uniforms at home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, but that was only when some exercises were organised. Then people would be issued uniforms for a period of 7 to 15 days. According to my knowledge, after the exercise, the uniforms would go back to the depot.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, just in relation to that: I think you indicated that you don't have any personal knowledge of the reserve situation, because I think you said you weren't in the reserves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So as far as you're aware, it may indeed be the situation that people kept their uniforms -- people who were in the reserves kept their uniforms at home.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that question I was asking you about Jovanovic: What was he actually wearing?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing an olive-drab military uniform. I believe that I have described it several times. I believe that this uniform belonged to the reserve troops of Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. And now, Mr. Hasanovic, you also indicated in your evidence that you went to the sports hall, the school building, the Vuk Karadzic building, and you said that three soldiers were torturing and killing people, whereas the others were either guarding the door or they were standing in the corridors or they were in front of the entrance to the school building. And you were asked this question: "Were these the same soldiers you described, that is -- described earlier, that is, local soldiers?" This is at page 21 of the transcript, Your Honour, from yesterday. And your answer was this: "The ones at the entrance and in front of the entrance were soldiers from the town of Bratunac and the neighbouring republic, and in the school itself, there were soldiers who identified themselves as Arkan's men. They told us that they were paid to do what they were doing. They also told us that they would make more money if they killed more people." Do you remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, these soldiers that were at the entrance and in front of the entrance, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing military uniforms that I have already described as belonging to the reserve military, and they mostly had rifles. Some of them had automatic rifles and there were even some who had semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the people who identified themselves as Arkan's men, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They mostly had pistols. I did not see any of them having rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, but what were they wearing in terms of clothes, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One soldier, whom I described as being the number one among them, the one who carried out murders, had an SMB olive-green/grey overalls, in fact. He had no headgear. He had an earring in his ear. And another soldier had the summer uniform which I described several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hasanovic. Now, you -- further on in your evidence yesterday, you indicated that you were taken in some lorries to Pale. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you said that you were escorted by the soldiers of Republika Srpska, dressed in military uniforms. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, can you describe that uniform for me?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have said quite a lot about that uniform. There were SMB, that is, olive-green/grey uniforms, and also camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's it?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Hasanovic, you recall when you commenced giving evidence yesterday that His Honour the Presiding Judge asked you to make a solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you recall that that solemn declaration is that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, of course, Mr. Hasanovic, you realise that this Court is here to hear the complete truth, not just what suits one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that this Tribunal takes the solemn declaration very seriously, as you do?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall when I asked you these questions yesterday: "Now, this other person, another person you've mentioned here, for example, Hasib Hasanovic." I asked you: How did he die? And you said: "Again, I heard that Hasib Hasanovic, who was the school principal, that he was killed. I heard that he was killed. However, I did not witness that. In my second statement that I gave to the OTP, I didn't mention him because I did not learn any additional information about him, so I couldn't be sure whether he was killed or not." Then I asked you who told you that he was killed. "I was told that by the people who were with me in the camp or exchanged, either in Visoko or in the hospital in Zenica. They told me that they heard that the school principal, Hasib, had also been killed." Then I asked you: "Now, Mr. Hasanovic, did you know Hasib Hasanovic?" You said: "Yes, I knew him but I did not have any contacts with him. I knew that he was the school principal. I knew of him." Then I asked you: "Now, of course, I think you realise, Mr. Hasanovic, that, obviously, some of the information you hear from other people can be mistaken or erroneous. You appreciate that fact, don't you?" And you said: "Yes, I'm absolutely clear on that." And then I said: "Because apparently Mr. Hasib Hasanovic --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, could you please slow down when you are reading, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I do apologise to the interpreters, Your Honour. I think I was going way too quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "Because apparently Mr. Hasib Hasanovic is alive and well and lives and works today in Tuzla as an educational inspector." That was my question. And your answer was: "Yes, I've heard that. I heard that later after I had given my statement to the OTP." Now, you recall those questions and answers yesterday, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, you did not tell the Court that Mr. Hasanovic was still alive and wasn't actually dead until you realised I knew he was alive. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say it, and nobody asked, anyway. In the statement that I gave to the investigators in Germany, I had not mentioned Hasib, and I did not know for sure that he was dead. I thought it was not necessary to speak any more about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, when I asked you the question: How did he die? You could have said: Well, actually, he's not dead. I learned that after I gave my second statement. But you didn't do that, did you, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember being asked that, and I don't remember these answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry? You don't remember being asked "How did he die?" yesterday, by me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read the transcript to the witness. Mr. Hasanovic, yesterday Ms. Loukas asked you: "Now, this other person, another person you've mentioned there, for example, Hasib Hasanovic." You said: "Yes." Then Ms. Loukas asked: "How did he die?" And your answer was: "Again, I heard that Hasib Hasanovic, who was the school principal, that he was killed. I heard that he was killed. However, I did not witness that. In my second statement that I gave to the OTP, I didn't mention him because I did not learn any additional information about him, so I couldn't be sure whether he was killed or not." That is the complete testimony, at least the relevant part. Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, you've heard His Honour the Presiding Judge read out that particular portion of your evidence yesterday. You didn't tell the Court he wasn't dead, did you, or that you'd heard he wasn't dead?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said exactly what the Honourable Judge has just read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, of course, when I asked you the question: "Now, of course, I think you realise, Mr. Hasanovic, that obviously some of the information you hear from other people can be mistaken or erroneous. You appreciate that fact, don't you?" And your answer was: "Yes. I'm absolutely clear on that." And you didn't say at that point either that: Yes, I realise that, because in 2000 I was told he wasn't dead. You didn't bother to mention it at that point, did you?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that, in my first and in my second, most important, statement, I did not mention Hasib Hasanovic, and I shouldn't have said a word about it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, of course, you'd been in contact with the Prosecution when you found out this additional information between the year 2000 and now. You didn't bother to tell them during that period?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Prosecution is concerned, I talked to them very briefly, and all of these discussions took place in the past month or two months. And we mainly discussed the terms of my arrival here, my travel.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. How about the proofing session that you had this week, which I think you gave evidence about earlier today, took about four or five hours? Do you recall that proofing session earlier this week?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: From which five pages of additional proofing notes were produced? Do you recall that proofing session?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I think the point you'd like to make is perfectly clear to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In that case, there's just a couple of questions left, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you didn't tell the Prosecution in the proofing session; I appreciate that. Now, but when you were in court and I asked you this question yesterday, when I was asking you about paragraph 1 of your March 2000 statement, I said: "And you pointed out in the statement that you gave the ICTY Prosecution investigators that you wanted to clarify something, and that was at the time of your statement. You'd made some references to men being dead but later you found out that they were actually alive." Do you recall that aspect of your statement? And then you went on to give a long answer. You said: "Yes, I do, and I will gladly clarify for you." And you described two men. And at the end of that answer you said: "Basically I'm talking about two men of Serb ethnicity that I was mistaken about." Do you recall that question and answer, Mr. Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But the fact is, Mr. Hasanovic, you were also mistaken about a Muslim man, and you didn't bother to mention him at that point.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I didn't bother because I was focusing on the things that are included in my statement that I had given to ICTY investigators here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Hasanovic, you were focusing on matters that might be helpful to the Muslim cause rather than the Serb cause. Perhaps that was what was on your mind, Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no thought of helping or blaming one side or the other. I thought that I should do my best to recount all that I had seen and experienced before this Honourable Court, in the best way I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just one further question, Mr. Hasanovic. In response to my question yesterday, when I said to you: "Because apparently Mr. Hasib Hasanovic is alive and well and lives and works today in Tuzla as an educational inspector"; and your answer was: "Yes, I've heard that. I heard that later, after I had given my statement to the OTP. When I visited Bosnia, I heard that Hasib was alive, but that was in the year 2000, in July or August, when I -- before I went to America." And then His Honour the Presiding Judge asked you a question. He said: "Would you allow me just to check. Is he one of the two persons you just mentioned that you said you learned later on that they were still alive, or is this a third person?" And your answer was: "That is a third person. In the meantime, I found out about him, between the first statement I gave to the Bosnian authorities and the second statement I gave to the ICTY investigators. He is the third person I learned about. That's why I didn't mention him before." Do you see that answer? Sorry. Do you recall that answer?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the answer, but I don't remember exactly that I said that I had heard about him between these two statements. I remember saying that I had heard about it after giving these two statements, when I was on a visit to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's page 73 of the transcript, Your Honours. So, in answer to my question, you say that you heard about it after you gave the statement to the Prosecution, but in answer to His Honour's question, you say that you heard about it between the two statements. So, Mr. Hasanovic, which is it?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that I heard about it between the two statements. It is quite possible that I wasn't expecting at all to be asked any questions apart from what is covered by my ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be helpful if Mr. Hasanovic is referred to the full text of his answer. I think Ms. Loukas has quoted to him part of his answer, but he provided a further clarification where in fact it seems that he stated something in respect of finding out information between two statements, and then immediately said: "-- after giving those two statements." So if that could be put to him in full, he may be able to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas. It's clear that the witness gave, on your first question, before we knew about whether there was a third person or not, he gave detailed information about when he learned it. And then when I asked him: "Is he one of the two persons you just mentioned that you say you learned later on that they are still alive, or is this a third person?" The witness said: "That is a third person. In the meantime, I found out about him between the first statement I gave to Bosnian authorities and the second statement I gave to ICTY investigators." And then it stops. Whatever, that's a sentence which seems to be not complete. And then he says: "He's the third person I learned about, so that's why I didn't mention him before." It is clear that there is some inconsistency in this answer. And if you wanted to draw our attention to that, you succeeded in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. That was the text of the answer I read out, so I'm not quite understanding the point that Mr. Margetts made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What part was missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, at a further juncture, if I may read from the text -- I don't think we have the same reference numbers on the text, so if I could just read from the text. He says -- the witness said: "I wouldn't say, though, that I made an error. I heard about two of these three people between two statements that I have given, and I found out about one more person after those two statements. And since that happened after I talked to the investigators, I haven't mentioned it until now." And he has mentioned three people; two Serbs and the third person being Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's, of course, not part of his first answer, and I did understand that Ms. Loukas wanted to focus and concentrate mainly on this answer given to my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, it would be helpful if I had the particular reference to that question that Mr. Margetts was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, that's, in my LiveNote, on page 74, line 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where he says: "I wouldn't say, though, that I made an error."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, you've heard me read out those -- the answer you gave me first. You've heard me read out the answer you gave His Honour. Now, you've heard the Prosecution read out the other answer; right? So in relation to my question, you're saying that it was in the year 2000, in July or August. In relation to His Honour's question, you're saying it was between the first statement and the second statement. In relation to a further question from me, where I say to you: "So when you referred to that correction in your statement, that being the correction in relation to the people dead but not dead, you referred to there being two people that you'd made an error about. But there's, in fact, a third person that you've made an error about, but you didn't refer to that in your evidence today. That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Hasanovic?" Your response was the response read out by Mr. Margetts: "Yes, I wouldn't say, though, that I made an error. I heard about two of these three people between two statements I have given, and I found out about one more after giving those two statements." So you're telling His Honour that it was between the two statements and you're telling me that it was after those two statements. Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally cannot put everything in exact chronology. But the gist of my statement was that I heard reliable information, verified information, about two people, according to which they were still alive, and I later heard about a third person, after giving two statements. And I said I was unwilling to say anything about that third person until I've checked personally myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Who did you say that to?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said this here, as part of my testimony at this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, the fact is, on your solemn declaration, you did not give the Court the whole truth. That's the situation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have said the truth to the best of my recollection, in the chronology as I could best remember it. If you ask me during the cross-examination about the third person, my answer could have been confusing, and you later asked me about another two people. The point is that I was unwilling to say anything about Hasib because I wasn't sure whether he was alive or dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, when you walked into this courtroom, you knew that he was alive.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew he was alive, but I never thought about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one very small matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if Mr. Hasanovic could be given a copy of his B/C/S proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, in the course of the examination by Ms. Loukas, you were asked about arms held by MUP members. Could I refer you to paragraph 2 of the proofing notes in front of you, in particular the second sentence of paragraph 2, and I'll read that to you: "Whilst they asked for the division to allegedly protect the Serbs, after two or three days, this appeared not to be their objective because they disarmed the Muslim members of the MUP and sent them home." Is that correct? After the division, did the Serbs disarm the Muslim members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you, Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I should like to ask you two little questions. The first concerns what you said about the time when you were in that sports hall. You said that a commander had come and ordered that you be given water and food. Do you remember who that commander was and to which unit he belonged?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly know who he was. He was an officer wearing a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. military uniform whom I hadn't seen in Bratunac until that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was the uniform of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you had the impression that the guards were not actually obeying orders; rather, everybody did as they pleased?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment when he entered the gym, the sports hall, he shouted at them at first: What are you doing to these people? or something like that. And he chased them away. And they obeyed him. But actually, those were not the guards. Those were the three men who carried out the murders, who did the killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we can deduce that those guards were not actually following orders; they were acting, so to speak, against the orders?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, those who did the killing were the guards, and in the presence of the troops, they -- sorry. In the absence of the army, they committed these crimes, and the army, when they found out about this, tried to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, in the absence of the troops, they did that, and when the army found out what had been going on, the army wanted to install some order; is that true?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then you received water and food?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but may I expand a little, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if you could do it in just a few words, please.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were very happy to see this officer, because we believed that he would save us, those of us who had remained alive. However, when they left, the people who had been killing returned and the situation continued until late in the evening on the third day. Then the troops returned and told us that we would no longer be ill-treated, that this would be the end of our sufferings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And another clarification, please. You said, in paragraph 24 of your statement -- I'm going to quote in English: [Previous translation continues]... [Interpretation] Can you please confirm a certain date or is it the case that you don't remember the exact date when this happened?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please be more specific as to what date are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 24 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the date when we were loaded onto the trucks and taken to Pale?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I'm going to quote in English: "The day after the police department split -- [In English] the Serbs were wearing their own Serbian uniforms..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Hasanovic has the B/C/S copy of his proofing notes before him and not a copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- statement. Mr. Hasanovic, there was some confusion about the document you had in front of you.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The exact date is something that I can't remember, but I believe that it was the 11th of April. I can't be sure, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, my point is as follows: Are you sure that on the following day, when you say on the following day, does that mean in the broader sense the following day?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we're talking about the sequence of events, it's very different to put them in a certain order. They were very quick developments, very sudden developments, but I believe that it was one or two days after the police department split, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, I have a few questions for you as well. You told us that at the entrance of the sports hall, there were the local soldiers, whereas in the school building there were Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they communicate with each other; and if so, how? Or were they operating totally independent of each other?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly what sort of communication they were using. The one standing at the door after their departure, or the moment when there was somebody at the door, they would tell us that they couldn't do anything, that they couldn't help us, that they couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is an indication of that Arkan's men were rather in control, and those at the door could not interfere in whatever way what happened inside; is that a correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what was going on between them. After their departure, the people at the door were much kinder to us, and they showed much more understanding towards us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Then, finally, I'd like to know exactly when for the first time you heard, whether it was a rumour, whether it was somebody who told you, about Mr. Hasib Hasanovic still be alive. So I'm not asking about whether you thought that information to be reliable at that moment, but when, for the very first time, you heard about Hasib Hasanovic still being alive.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard that was when I went to Bosnia in July 2000. I heard it from a friend in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From a friend in Tuzla. Were you in Tuzla at that time or did he give you a phone call from Tuzla? You were in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Tuzla, and in random conversations I learned that Hasib was alive. I didn't know where he was, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not know that he was in Tuzla at that very moment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This friend of yours who told you, was he from Bratunac or was he from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were people from Bratunac, but they had resided in Tuzla for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what was the occasion that caused them to tell you that Hasib Hasanovic was still alive? Was it -- were you discussing schools? Were you discussing people that had disappeared? Were you discussing -- what was the context in which it came up?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were talking about everything: People who had been detained, exchanged information about the camps that they were detained, and Hasib Hasanovic's name came up in one of those conversations. Somebody said that he was alive and that he was somewhere, alive and well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually, you emphasise that someone is alive if one would think that a person is dead. Did you indicate something about his death or that you heard about his death?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I spoke about the statement that I gave to the ICTY, and within that context, I said that I didn't know anything about Hasib's lot. To my question, my friend replied that Hasib was alive and that the information that I had was incorrect, that it was not true that the school principal Hasib Hasanovic had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Did the questions of the Bench trigger any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same for the Prosecution, as I see from nodding. Mr. Hasanovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you for having answered a lot of questions from both parties and from the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

To the extent that could create confusion, I tried to compare how a U is written in this handwriting and now an A is written in this handwriting. And it seems to me, at first sight, that there's an error in the transcript into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until 10 minutes past 11.00. And may I take it, then, that the Prosecution will call its next witness? Yes. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes past 11.00.

I don't know whether -- you're not obliged to give an answer, but you put a question to the witness in respect of an incident that took place in Kravica where two Serbs were killed. But you -- it appears that you had something else in mind. If you'd like to -- if it's unknown to us, you can just keep it the way it is, or we'll hear what evidence the Defence would come up in the near future -- or in the later future, but it just -- it did not ring a bell, at least not to me. So if you'd say: Okay, that's fine, then we leave it as it is. If there's any confusion, then perhaps you could help us out.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, there's no confusion, Your Honour. That's a matter that obviously we will be attending to in the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll wait and see what happens, yes. Your next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check it right away, and if I made a mistake, I apologise for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll do it at a later stage.

utterances.text: I'll do it at a later stage, Ms. Loukas. Good morning, Mr. Alic. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alic. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alic. Mr. Alic --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- I'm going to ask you questions about your background. I'm going to ask you merely to verify the data that I give you. Let me give you the data and then ask you to verify it. You were born on 7 February 1955, you're a Bosniak, you're married and have four children, you were born in the village --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Don't answer me, Mr. Alic, until I've finished giving you all of the data and then I'll merely ask for a single answer to verify what I've given you. You were born in the village of Blagaj Japra in the municipality of Bosanski Novi, where you lived until 1992, when you became a refugee. Your schooling consisted of primary school and later you passed an examination for being a merchant. In Blagaj Japra, you and your wife had a small grocery store. Is that information correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you were in the JNA for 15 months and you served in the years 1973 and 1974, and you suffer a physical disability, which is the permanent loss of the sight in one eye as a result of events which you will be describing to this Trial Chamber; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, I'd like to present my first exhibit, which is a statement of Mr. Alic. It is an English and B/C/S statement that was given by Mr. Alic on the 12th of March, 2000. In this statement of yours, Mr. Alic -- a copy of the B/C/S version will be placed in front of you. It has numbered paragraphs and copies of the English version of the statement will be distributed to the Judges and to the parties. And while these statements are being distributed, Mr. Alic, would you kindly take a look at the statement in B/C/S in front of you and just examine it.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. You want me to look at the front page only?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Alic, let me ask you in just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, could I get an exhibit number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is P76, and the translation P76.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, in front of you is P76.1, which is a statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 12th of March, 2000. Could you just take a look at that statement, the whole statement, very quickly, and confirm that that is the statement that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor and you signed. You don't have to read the whole thing; just glance through it and confirm that the statement in front of you is your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While Mr. Alic is reviewing his statement, Your Honour, may I get an estimated time when we will conclude the first -- when we will next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next break will presumably be at approximately a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, have you reviewed that statement and is the Prosecution Exhibit 76.1 your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have reviewed it, and yes, it is my statement, signed by me on the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And other than some minor corrections, which we will make in the course of your examination, does this recount the events accurately?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I am going to proceed under Rule 89(F), and with this statement, but I'd like to summarise the written evidence of that statement before I start to go into clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll summarise the statement now. Mr. Alic is a Bosniak who was born in the village of Blagaj Japra, which is located in the Japra valley in the municipality of Novi Travnik. The village --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I mixed my Novis up. Bosanski Novi. This village consists of approximately 500 houses and approximately 2.500 inhabitants at the time when Mr. Alic was residing there. He lived in that village until the 9th of June, when he, his family, the other villagers from that village, and Muslim refugees who had been removed from other Muslim villages and who were residing in the village, were all forcibly expelled from Blagaj Japra. The statement, in part, touches on some background before the conflict and describes, in part, an event in March of 1992, when a neighbour of Mr. Alic's who was a Muslim policeman from the town of Bosanski Novi was dismissed from his position because he refused to wear a uniform that had a Serb insignia. During the period prior to the conflict, there was a conflict going on in Croatia which was adjacent to the municipality boundary of Novi Travnik. The Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this again Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I keep saying -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. The Muslims in Blagaj Japra refused to participate in the war in Croatia, and there was a deterioration of the relations. As a result, the Muslims, according to Mr. Alic, were perceived as enemies of the Serbs. Additionally, Serb nationalistic songs were transmitted on the radio and Serbs started to say that what had happened to the Croats would happen to the Muslims. This and other provocations by the Serbs caused fear in the Muslim community. On the 9th of May, 1992, Serbs announced over Bosanski Novi radio an ultimatum that all Muslims were required to turn in their weapons. The ultimatum demanded that weapons be turned in the next day. The following day, which was the 10th of May, the SDA president of Blagaj Japra, Izet Mehmedagic, collected a small number of weapons - these were hunting rifles and pistols - from the villagers and took them to the Bosanski Novi municipality building. Those weapons were not accepted by the authorities, and Mr. Mehmedagic returned to the village with the weapons. That same night, a military police car was attacked. Mr. Alic did not see that attack and who attacked the police car is somewhat in dispute. Later that same night, the village of Blagaj Japra was shelled by mortars. Approximately 13 shells landed in the village. The next morning, the 11th of May, 1992, the witness's father and cousin went to an adjacent Serb village of Radomirovac and asked the Serbs in that village why Blagaj Japra had been shelled. They were told by the Serbs that the village had been shelled because the Muslims had not handed in their weapons. Later that day, Blagaj Japra was again shelled. This time the barrage was far more intense: Approximately 300 shells landed around the village. And Mr. Alic and his family took shelter in the cellar of his home. Sometime that day, a Muslim man who is identified in the statement came by the witness's house on his tractor and told Mr. Alic and his family to go to the nearby village, Serbian village, of Maslorave [phoen]. A caravan of trucks and tractors and cars was formed, with approximately 1.000 Muslims, residents, in that caravan, and they then progressed in the direction of Maslovare. En route to that Serbian village, the caravan was stopped by a barricade -- stopped at a barricade and the Muslims in the caravan were disarmed of their hunting rifles and allowed to proceed. They arrived at their destination and spent the night, some of them under the sky, some of them in barns. The following morning, military personnel arrived at the witness's location. The villagers asked to be allowed to return to Blagaj Japra, and a small group of Muslims were allowed to return to the village. When they came back, they reported that the Serbs had raised Serb flags in their village. Thereafter, the witness and other villagers were allowed to return to Blagaj Japra. En route back to Blagaj Japra, the witness observed in the adjacent village, which is known as Blagaj Rijeka, which is a very short distance from his village, that the mosque in Blagaj Rijeka was completely destroyed and that the mosque in his village was damaged. The damage was damage to the minaret. After returning to his village, the witness stayed in Blagaj Japra for about 15 days. During this period of time, other Muslim villages in the Japra valley were shelled. A summer house belonging to a Serb located near the Serbian village of Maslovare was blown up, and a Muslim house was blown up. His village was hit with semi-automatic weapon fire. Following the shelling of the surrounding Muslim villages, the inhabitants of those villages were told by members of the Serb Territorial Defence to go to Blagaj Japra, and they did. They reported that their houses had been burned. The number of people in the small village of Blagaj Japra swelled considerably as a result of the influx of these displaced people. Thereafter, negotiations between the representatives of the Muslim communities, the villages of Blagaj Japra and the other villages from where the displaced persons had come, and the Serbs took place in the Bosanski Novi municipal building. These negotiations lasted approximately 17 days. According to the witness's statement, the Serbs wanted the Muslims to leave the municipality. The next event of importance in the statement is that on the 8th of June, 1992, two Serb soldiers informed the occupants of Blagaj Japra, not only occupants, but the people who had been displaced and who were living in the village at the time, that they had to leave the village the next morning. The following morning, Serb soldiers came to Mr. Alic's house and told him and the other occupants of the house that they had to leave the house. That order was complied with. The witness and others were taken to the village elementary school and detained at that location under threat of arms, but later that day permitted to leave and put out on the street. Mr. Alic, after leaving, was able to see in his village burning houses and barns as he transited. As the witness and his family went through the village, Serb soldiers murdered his brother and another man who he can identify. Both those murders took place in the witness's presence. Later, Mr. Alic observed Serb soldiers kill three other Muslim men. And later yet, the witness and other Muslims, as they transited the village, were robbed of their valuables by Serb soldiers. Mr. Alic and others were then ordered to go to the Japra factory, and that is a factory that is located near railroad tracks. And at that location, the witness was informed that Serbs would take him and other Muslims to Zenica and exchange them with the Serb population from that village and would move -- and those people who were displaced from Zenica would move to Blagaj Japra. At the factory, Mr. Alic observed the soldiers shoot and kill another Muslim man. At the Japra factory, he and the other people who had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been displaced - and there's a number that we'll correct in the course of the examination, but thousands, they numbered thousands - he and other Muslim men, women, and children were loaded onto cattle cars which were standing on the railroad tracks near the factory and transported out of the municipality. The train later stopped in the village of Stanari, which is near Doboj, and there the army and the military police separated the men from the women and placed the men and women on separate trains. There will be a correction in respect of that that I have just mentioned. The train, with the witness and other men, stopped at Omarska and Keraterm and ultimately returned to Bosanski Novi. In Bosanski Novi, the witness and approximately 750 men remained on the train cars for approximately two days. During those two days, there was no food, no water, no toilets. And thereafter, the train went to Mlakve. It arrived there on the 11th of June. Mlakve is a suburb of the town of Bosanski Novi, and there the witness and approximately 750 men were taken to a football stadium, where they were detained. At their detention location, the football stadium, the food was insufficient. The witness describes one kilogramme of bread and weak soup for ten men per day. No blankets were provided. The witness and others slept in the dressing-rooms of the stadium on tile floors. There was no soap, no hot water, two toilets for 750 men. While detained at the Mlakve stadium, Mr. Alic was struck in the eye by a rifle butt, a Serb soldier struck him in the eye and he was permanently blinded as a result of that strike. He did not receive medical treatment for his injury while he was in captivity. He arrived at the camp weighing 75 kilos, and when he was released, he weighed 55 kilogrammes. While he was at the camp, Mlakve stadium, he was never told why he was arrested or why he had been taken to the camp. Before leaving the camp, he was told that if he wanted to leave, he had to sign a document saying that he was leaving Bosanski Novi municipality voluntarily, and he had to sign away his property. After he signed such a document, he was released on the 27th of July, 1992. He was placed on a bus, taken to Croatia, where he rejoined his family and he then left and became a refugee living in a third country. The testimony in this statement relates to items of the indictment that have been described in the 65 ter summary. In addition, Your Honour, specifically his testimony relates to paragraph 3.1 in schedule A; in schedule C points 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3; and in schedule D, points 3.6 and 3.9. That concludes my summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. I take it that you want to go to more detail --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I wish to at this point clarify other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As we indicated yesterday, the Chamber would very much like to receive the statements which are summarised prior to the hearing itself so that we can prepare as well. So that's not for this moment but for the near future.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the next exhibit, please, and it should appear on the monitor. If a hard copy could be shown to the witness. Since most of these -- since all of -- I should say since most of the testimony of Mr. Alic relates to the municipality of Bosanski Novi, I just want to place Bosanski Novi in location in respect of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Alic, can you confirm for the Trial Chamber that the next exhibit properly shows the location of Bosanski Novi in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
