utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is here in the corner, near to the border with Croatia, and it is painted red.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And could I have the exhibit number for that particular Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P77.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, since -- I'd like to show you one other map, Mr. Alic, since most of your testimony will relate to the Japra valley in Bosanski Novi municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the next exhibit distributed and a copy placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P78.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please be provided with a copy of the Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have any extra copy? Otherwise the Bench would certainly -- here's another copy. Yes, there's a spare copy, so if that could be provided to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed -- yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. That's very helpful, in fact, because we only have a black and white copy and it's more readable on the colour copy for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever another copy -- I see you have a coloured copy now as well, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, I'd like you to confirm what I'm going to say. Did you assist me in the preparation of this particular exhibit by identifying for me the villages in the Japra valley that were essentially Muslim villages, and are those villages Blagaj Rijeka, Blagaj Japra, Suhaca, Hodzici, and Gornji Agici, and they are all marked in green? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you indicate for me which villages in the Japra valley were mixed Muslim and Serb villages, and are those villages of Maslovare, Crna Rijeka, Donji Agici, and are they marked in pink?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the villages that are unmarked, such as Radomirovac and Krslje and Josava, those are Serb villages, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. All these are Serb villages. Ruzicka [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Rujiska maybe. The interpreter isn't sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic -- now, Mr. Alic, I'd like you to take the copy of the statement that is in front of you, copy -- Prosecution Exhibit 76.1. Do you have the statement in front of you? I'm going to refer you to certain paragraphs that are numbered and I'm going to ask you for certain clarifications. So if you could take your statement in B/C/S, and the first paragraph I'm going to deal with is paragraph 3 on the statement. And this paragraph, Mr. Alic, relates to a neighbour who was a policeman, who told you that the police had received new Serb police uniforms with Serb insignias. My question to you is: Who is that individual?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: That was Mirso Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he a neighbour of yours in Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he agree to wear the new Serb uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. He refused, and the others also refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Brkic was a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was he dismissed from the police force and was he later expelled from the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. All Bosniaks, Muslims, who worked for the police were dismissed, chased out, just as I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to have you turn your attention to paragraph 12. This particular paragraph, Mr. Alic, deals with trucks that went through your village every second day with ammunition. And your statement says: "We could only guess they were preparing something. I did not see when the Serbs distributed weapons among themselves." Let me take you a little outside of that paragraph and say: Did you ever see any helicopters land in the Japra valley?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I saw that. Like villages Radomirovac, Krslje, and some other places I cannot recall right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were you able to see what was in those helicopters or what those helicopters were doing in those Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't see. They would land, and after half an hour, an hour, they would take off again. But since it was a military helicopter, I suppose it transported some military equipment, ammunition, weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was this -- these sightings of the helicopters landing in the Serb villages that you've identified, was that before the shooting began, before your village was attacked, or after?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Before. That happened before that village was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you have occasion at some point in time, Mr. Alic, to be in the village of Maslovare and actually see ammunition in boxes?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: During the time when we were detained at Rajko Hodzic's estate --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we are in a situation whereby the statement has been tendered, the witness is in the witness box. I think it's inappropriate for the Prosecutor to lead on an area such as this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before we continue: You consistently are telling us about the village Maslorave, where as it's consistently put on the record that it's Maslovare, which is not the same. I take it that you agree that it's Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whenever you pronounce it again in the V and the R mixing up, then it will be put in the record as Maslovare.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see any weapons or ammunitions at any point in time prior to the shooting that occurred in your village?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. No, I couldn't -- I wasn't able to see that. I didn't see anything before it was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can re-frame the question. Did you have an occasion --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might just object again at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The situation is, as I've already indicated, the statement's been tendered, the witness is in the witness box, he has his statement in front of him, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd rather have not the statement in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Alic, could you perhaps -- your statement, what you've told us that it's your statement, just put it a bit aside because you're now examined --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can do that. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, let me focus your attention, Mr. Alic. Did you have occasion to be in the Serb village of Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I don't understand exactly. Do you mean before we were attacked or later?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before you were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did go to Suhaca and to other places. I moved around freely, normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were in any of the Serb villages, did you have occasion to see, in any of the Serb villages, any armaments, weapons, or ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that question, certainly the question in relation to ammunition has already been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I -- there's some confusion on the part of the witness. I think I should be permitted to ask him that question again. I will refresh his recollection with his previous sworn testimony, if that's going to be an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if we would strictly adhere to question asked, question answered, we would save a lot of time in this courtroom. I'll allow you to do it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Please, could you repeat that again? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you were in the village of Maslovare, did you have an occasion to see any ammunition or weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, not before the war, not before it all began, before my village was attacked. I saw that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us about what you saw later.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, when we were coming back from Rajko Hodzic's place the next day, we came to the shop owned by Mico Karlica, and Mico Karlica personally stopped me and said: You did not turn over your pistol. Before the end of this day, you have to bring it here, together with your licence. He offered me a beer. I couldn't refuse, because he had a couple of drinks already. He brought me another beer. I had that one too. I asked him to use the bathroom in his shop, and he told me to go instead and use the field latrine behind his house. When I went there, it was not really a toilet. It was some sort of shed covered by paper or cardboard, and as these planks were put together, you could see through them. And looking through these planks, I saw some boxes with military equipment in them. I was not sure whether it was ammunition or weapons, but I saw a lot of military equipment in those boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Let's proceed. I'd like to direct your attention further to paragraph 13, where you describe, in the first part of that paragraph -- I will read it: "On the 9th May 1992, it was a Saturday, the Serbs announced over Bosanski Novi radio that all Bosniaks should turn over their weapons." I have two questions for you, Mr. Alic. Did you personally hear that ultimatum on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. We heard that with our own ears, and even from Maslovare, Ranko Gvozden came, as far as I remember, together with other man whose name I can't recall right now. These two came to the village and told us that we had to comply, we had to turn over the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did the ultimatum apply to Muslims only? Did it apply to Serbs? Did it apply to Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. It applied only to Muslims, because Blagaj Japra was populated by Muslims alone. There were no Serbs or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm talking about the ultimatum you heard on the radio. Did the ultimatum you heard on the radio apply only to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: The same thing that I heard from Ranko Gvozden, I heard again in the form of a radio announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, further to clarify what's in paragraph 13: You describe the following day a meeting that took place at a school, where, and I quote your statement: "We collected some weapons, but not too many." Can you inform the Trial Chamber the number of weapons that were collected and the types of weapons that were collected.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, it was mainly hunting rifles and pistols, for which people had licences, 15 or 20 rifles, a dozen pistols, et cetera. There were no other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 16, I would like to direct your attention, and I will read the portion of the paragraph I'm interested in: "That night, at about 2330, our village was shelled. 13 mortar shells hit the village." Now, was that attack, Mr. Alic, the same day that the weapons that had been collected were rejected by the authorities in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: That happened on that same day, that those weapons were turned over but they just laughed and said it is not the amount that we expected and that we need. And they brought -- and he -- the man who brought the weapon took it home, took it back home. However, around 11.00, the police patrol between Bosanski Novi and Blagaj Japra was allegedly attacked. However, it was not a Muslim-organised attacked. It was orchestrated by the Serbs themselves, who threw a hand-grenade, opened a volley of automatic fire, and pretended that it was an attack. That happened in -- after that, 20 minutes later, shelling began, targeting Svorno [phoen]. I believe that it was all prepared in advance, because they couldn't have put up that artillery within 20 minutes and started shelling just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me focus on something you said. You said that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just a point of clarification on the transcript, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm informed by my case manager that this bit that was translated here - where is it? - it was translated into English as: "It is not the amount that we expected and that we need." That's what was translated into English. However, as I understand it, that is not what was actually said in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask the witness. Mr. Alic, what was the response when these weapons were delivered and, as you said, taken back again later on? What did they actually say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Izet Mehmedagic brought this back to us and said that they had only laughed. They said: That's not what we asked you for. We asked from you to bring heavy weapons, not only hunting rifles and pistols. We want other weapons. We didn't have any other weapons. We had only those for which we had licences. But those people said -- only laughed and said: This is not enough. Take that back.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' apologies. We have difficulty understanding the witness sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever you have difficulties, for the interpreters, then of course I could always ask the witness to repeat his answer so that it becomes clearer. I do take it that it was amount rather than the type of weapons which caught your attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My case manager indicated to me that the translation was not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, in part of your answer you described an attack on a military police vehicle or patrol. And your answer and your description of that is based not on your personal observations but what other people told you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, again, focusing on this first attack on your village that took place later that night, to your knowledge, was anybody in your village firing back at the locations where these shells were coming from, or, in your view, was this a situation that was a combat situation?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I think it's inappropriate to lead. I think the first part of the question is unobjectionable, but to go on and express a potential view is, in my submission, inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that it's rather a conclusion what kind of situation it is. But could you please answer the question whether there was any fire coming back from the places that were shelled. Was there any return fire from those places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody fired. After we had surrendered all our weapons, we had nothing to fire from. Nobody fired a single bullet against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me take you to paragraph 17, Mr. Alic. And this describes the following morning after the attack on your village, and it says: "The following morning, Jasim Alic and Camil Alic and some other neighbours went over to the village of Radomirovac and asked them why the shelling happened." Can you identify the relationship -- can you identify your relationship to Jasmin [phoen] Alic and Camil Alic.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Jasim, not Jasmin, Alic. He's my father. Camil Alic, however, is a relative, Camil, C-A-M-I-L.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. And moving on to paragraph 18. This describes the attack on your village where approximately 300 shells were launched. Can you tell us, approximately how long did the shelling of your village on that occasion last?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: The attack started around 10.00, when my father and Camil Alic had not yet arrived at the house. They had already started shelling. It was around 10.00, 10.30 and lasted until around 3.00 or 4.00 p.m., until we got out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you and members of your family once again take shelter in your cellar?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. While they shelled, we spent all that time in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was anybody in your village firing weapons back?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, nobody did. Against such an armed force, it didn't cross our minds to return fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. We can turn to another part of paragraph 18. Let me ask you for a clarification. This paragraph describes then the arrival of Hamdija Selmic and the formation of a convoy, and approximately a thousand people getting into that convoy and going away from your village. The question I have for you is: First of all, did these people, a thousand people, were they only from your village or were they from an adjacent village as well?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Not only from our villages. From Blagaj Japra too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were they from? What other villages?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said, "No, only from Blagaj Japra."

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: The other villages, Suhaca and Kozica had not been attacked yet. It was only Blagaj Japra.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there anybody from Blagaj Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: From Blagaj Rijeka, people escaped to another village above or overlooking our village. It was called Dervisi, a Serbian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Paragraph 21, Mr. Alic. You -- to put this into context, you spent the night at Rajko Hodzic's house, you spent the night there under the sky and some slept in barns, and the next morning, according to the statement that is in evidence, it says: "The following morning, about 10 small military trucks arrived." Do you want to make a correction as to the number and the types of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, they were not trucks. Those were those small jeeps. Four or five persons can fit into one such jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber how the people who were in those jeeps were dressed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms, military camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to paragraph 22. I'd like you to expand a bit on what's in paragraph 22. Your evidence -- your written evidence says that a group of men were allowed to go to your village, Blagaj Japra, and they informed -- they returned and they informed you and the others that "the Serbs had erected Serb flags in our village." Were you told anything else about those flags?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They told us that we were free to go to our homes, that they had hoisted their flags, and if anybody attempts to take those flags down, they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "they," who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Those soldiers, our neighbours dressed as soldiers, who were going about the village, who were going into the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, which I will read, you said: "When we were on our way home, we could see that the houses in our village were burning. I saw that the mosque in Blagaj Rijeka was burning. The mosque in Blagaj Japra was hit with a mortar, but the minaret was still standing. The two villages were neighbouring villages, divided only by the river." My first question is: How many houses in those two villages were burning?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Approximately three to four houses, and the mosque. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the mosque in Blagaj Rijeka, what was its construction? What was it made of?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: It was made of wood. And since it was made of wood, both the mosque and the minaret had burnt. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed this word.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: -- was made of concrete. It was not destroyed and it was not damaged by fire, and it remained standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what exactly was made of concrete, because the interpreters missed a word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The minaret was made -- the tower, the minaret, the made of concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can clarify it, Your Honour, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there -- you described a wooden mosque in Blagaj Rijeka. Was there also a mosque in Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was one. That's the one I said was hit. But the minaret wasn't destroyed. It was hit, but the minaret remained standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And so when you referred to a minaret, or a concrete mosque, that was the mosque in Blagaj Japra; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... clarified, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I could have the next exhibit, please. Was the mosque in Blagaj Japra -- what happened to the mosque in Blagaj Japra after it had been damaged?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: This is where the mosque was. While I was in the camp in Mlakve, you can see that it was completely destroyed. I didn't see who destroyed it or when. In any case, it was during -- while I was detained that this mosque was razed to the ground. And you can only see its foundations, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the witness has just been referring to the exhibit unnumbered as yet, but that was handed to him. So if I could have a number on this, we can then --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, it bears a date on it. Could you, either through the witness or by informing the Chamber, explain what the date means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be glad to do that later, Your Honour. I don't have an explanation for it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you also take care that this exhibit is already on our screen, at least on the video -- on the computer screen already for some ten minutes. Could we wait -- because usually I do not move to another channel. Could we wait to put on the screen new exhibits until they are introduced. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For your information, this exhibit relates to schedule D3.6 in the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this, Mr. Alic, is what is left of the mosque in Blagaj Japra; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what is left, just the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to paragraph 25. And I will read paragraph 25. It's very short: "The following days, other Muslim villages were shelled. We could hear that." Now, that's the part I want some additional information on, Mr. Alic. Were you in contact at that time with villagers in other Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. My mother was born in Suhaca. I had some other relatives in Vozici [phoen], and I spoke to them on the phone and they told us that Suhaca had been attacked and Lozici [phoen], Agici, all of those after Blagaj Japra. They would first attack those villages, they would seize weapons. They did the same in these villages as they did in Blagaj Japra before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. To your knowledge, Mr. Alic, did the Muslim villages in the villages that you have identified have mosques in them?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a mosque in Suhaca and Vozici, in Donji Agici, in Gornji Agici, and all of them were destroyed, just as the one in Blagaj Japra was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we can focus our attention on paragraph 26. I will read it. Again, it's very short. I will ask you for some additional information: "After they had finished with all of the surrounding villages, and I mean after they had shelled them, they made all those residents go to Blagaj Japra." Approximately how many people from those villages came to Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Approximately 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And your statement goes on to say: "We asked them what happened, and they told us their houses were being burned and that the Serbs from the Serb TO told them to go to Blagaj Japra." That is again in paragraph 26. How long did those people who had been displaced from the other Muslim villages stay in Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Approximately 15 to 17 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And indeed, you had an opportunity, did you not, to talk to them about the events that had happened in their villages?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. My two mother's brothers lived there. They stayed in my house, and also some relatives from Vozici, and they told us everything that had happened; the same things that had happened to us, happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the next paragraph, you describe negotiating with the Serbs in Bosanski Novi municipality building, and can you tell me -- first of all, you didn't participate in those negotiations personally, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who were the negotiators?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Izet Mehmedagic and Sifet Bajraktarevic. Sifet Bajraktarevic was the president of the SDA in Suhaca, and Izet Mehmedagic was the president of the SDA in Blagaj Japra.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And would they keep you informed as to what was happening in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. The request was for the people to return to their homes; however, this was not allowed. It was obvious that this was a case of ethnic cleansing, as simple as that. They just wouldn't allow people to return to their homes during the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did they say? What was reported to you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Izet and Sifet told us what had been told to them, and that was that we wouldn't be allowed to return to our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me go to paragraph 28, the second sentence in that says that: "On the 8th of June, 1992, at around 1700, Ranko Gvozden and Mico Dolic told us we should be ready at 7.00 the following morning, as we had to leave the village." Can you tell me, Mr. Alic, who Ranko Gvozden and Mico Dolic are?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They were locals of Maslovare village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So they were Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were Serbs. And they were not officers, they just wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 29. You describe in this paragraph that Serb soldiers came to your house that particular morning. They were looking for your brother and others, and "they told us to leave the house." Now, how were those people dressed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Some wore masks on their faces. Some didn't. Some wore military uniforms. Some wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, later in that same paragraph, Mr. Alic, you talk about seeing a tank surrounded by Serb soldiers, people from reserve unit forces. Was the removal of people from your village, did it appear to you to be organised or did it appear to be a random event carried out by paramilitary organisations?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: It was organised. Everything was organised. First, the entire Japra Valley was pushed into Blagaj Japra, and then everybody who found themselves in Blagaj Japra was moved forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, 29, you said that after you had been taken to the elementary school and then released from the elementary school and put on the street, that you, and I quote: "When we walked out, we saw that the houses and barns were burning." Can you give us any idea of how many houses, how many barns were burning?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: A lot. Everything up to the school was ablaze. That's as far as they reached. Not only houses, but barns, stables, haystacks. Everything was ablaze.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And during this occasion when you were taken out of your house and while you were in the school and while you were then put on the street and walking, did you hear any shooting?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was shooting from all over the place; from the hilltops, from everywhere. It was Serbs that were shooting at us. They may have not been targeting us. I believe that they did it just to intimidate us, not really to shoot at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, turning your attention to paragraph 36. Eventually, Mr. Alic, your evidence, your written evidence says that you had been ordered by soldiers to go to the Japra company area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have the next exhibit, please. I'd like to show you a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will first give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P80.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, do you recognise what is depicted in photograph P80?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: This is the area that is called Japra.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And is this the area where you and thousands of other Muslims who had been displaced from the village found themselves before being transported out of the municipality on trains?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, we all gathered here, in this perimeter of the Japra company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And from this location, you were put on trains; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think that in fact it already formed part of the last question, and in that sense it is repetitive. Of course, we're all known to be repetitive in court, but there really is not any point in the next question, and in any event, it's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it's for me to determine whether there's a point to the question. And second of all, there are some leading questions that lead to additional questions. And that's a preliminary question to get to another area of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, as far as the repetition is concerned, the witness asked -- answered half of the question, so I would think that there's no reason to object against putting the second part of the question again to him in order to receive an answer. I do agree with you that it's leading. On the other hand, we have, of course, a relatively detailed statement which it's not -- it could not bring the attention of the witness to a possible answer where it has already been read to him. So in respect of leading, I do agree with you that to some extent it's leading, but under the present circumstances, I think it's not inadmissible. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This photograph, by the way, Your Honours, relates to schedule C, 5.1 in that schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, are the railroad tracks near this particular building that is depicted in Prosecutor Exhibit P80?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the left-hand side, only you can't see them in the photos. There are railroad tracks, and there's also a road leading to Prijedor. This is the Prijedor-Bosanski Novi main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in paragraph 39, your evidence is that: "Then the Serbs told us that they would take us to Zenica and exchange us with the Serb population in that village, and they would --" and it says, "moved [sic] in our village." Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Mico Dolic told me that. He wore military uniform. He was drinking coffee. I asked him: Mico, where are we being taken? And he said: You are being to Zenica to the places from which Serbs had been moved, and these Serbs are going to come to your villages. It was Mico Dolic who told me all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that the same individual who had also conveyed the message that you had to leave your village, earlier that day?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ranko Gvozden and Mico Dolic were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, from this particular location, and paragraph 40 I'm referring to, it says: "Around 6.00 or 7.00 in the evening, they loaded us -- all of us in cattle wagons which stood outside the company." Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Serbs, neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how were they dressed, those Serb neighbours who loaded you on these cattle wagons?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Camouflage military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you the next exhibit, if I could.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P81.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Will you tell us, Mr. Alic, what is depicted in P81.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: You can see the trains similar to the ones that carried us. They were open carriages and closed carriages. People were -- men were loaded onto open carriages and women and children onto closed carriages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were loaded onto these cattle cars that you described?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Approximately a hundred. It depended on the carriage. I didn't count heads, but the carriages were loaded, fully loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me direct your attention to paragraph 41. You say in this evidence: "I would say there were about 20.000 people." Just a minute ago you answered approximately 100. My question to you is, Mr. Alic: How many people in total were loaded onto train cars?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: About 15.000 altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you want to correct, then, what is in paragraph 41. It should be approximately 15.000 and not 20.000 people. Now, let me --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, about 15.000. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When people were loaded onto those cattle cars and those train cars, was any of the necessities of life provided to them? Was there food? Was there water? Was there blankets and protective garments from the elements? Were there sanitary facilities provided to the people who had been loaded on these train cars?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: There was nothing. They loaded us on the train just as they would a load of cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the people who were loaded on the train cars, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were the ages of the people who were loaded on those train cars?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: There were children, there were toddlers, there were one-year-old babies, and there were also 80-year-old elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, could you have refused to go on the train cars?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. No. We didn't have a choice. We had to get on the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were people -- strike that question. Okay. Besides Mr. Dolic telling you information, you personally information about where you might be going, were there any general announcements made to the approximately 15.000 people, where they were going, what would happen to them, when they would arrive?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: He said that we were being taken to Zenica to stay on forever, and that the Serbs would come to Blagaj Japra. But this was not the case. This was the case of ethnic cleansing, because we never returned to where we came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention, Mr. Alic, to paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that last question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Obviously, the answer is not responsive to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure -- if that's an objection, I think it's fair for the witness to conclude that when he and 15.000 other people are placed on cattle cars and permanently removed from their municipality, a characterisation of ethnic cleansing is a perfectly appropriate answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But, of course, ultimately, Your Honour, the characterisation is a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas. You could expect from the Chamber that if a witness describes a factual situation and adds to that what, in his view, that means in more general terms, that of course the Chamber will not take that as something that it should accept. It forms its own opinion on these kind of matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention - I'm sorry, Mr. Alic - to paragraph 41. In this paragraph, Mr. Alic, once -- to put it in context, once the people were loaded on the trains and the train departed to travel, and I quote: "We travelled the whole night, and early in the morning the train stopped in the village of Stanari, which is close to Doboj. We were ordered to go out." And the next paragraph says: "Army and military police arrived and they again started to separate us. They loaded all men on one train, and women were loaded to another one." Let me focus first on "they loaded all men on one train, and women were loaded to another one." How many men were separated and put in certain trains, and how many people were separated and put in another set of train cars? And let me re-phrase that. That's a poorly phrased question. Were all the men, approximately 15.000 people who had been placed on the train cars, were all the men separated or only some of the men separated from the other occupants of those train cars?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Only able-bodied men were separated. The elderly and the minors were not separated. They remained with the women and the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And approximately how many military-age men were separated and placed on separate train cars?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Approximately 750, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were you one of the 750 -- approximately 750 people separated and placed in separate train cars?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I was indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me focus first your attention on not the group of 750 but the other people who had been separated and placed on train cars. Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: As we were loaded onto the cars, they closed the doors and we didn't know what happened to the others, we didn't know what would happen to us. They closed the door so we couldn't see where we were being taken. We could see very little through the bars, and we could only guess that we were returning, returning in the direction of Banja Luka. We didn't know anything about what was happening with the women and the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to the women -- let me strike that. Was your wife and were your children separated from you and placed in a different set of cars?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what happened to your wife and children and the other people who were with them?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We didn't know at that time. We didn't know where they went. We didn't receive any information as to where they were being taken and what would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did your wife later tell you what happened to her and to your children and to the others?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once we were rejoined in Karlovac, once when I was released from the camp, she told me that they were first taken to Doboj and then transferred to Croatia, to Slavonska Pozega, and from there they were transported to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened then to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I just interrupt you. How much time you think you would still need? Because you asked an indication from my side when we would have our first break. That's approximately the time. But if you'd finish in a couple of minutes, then we could continue. Otherwise, we have to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think we should have the break now. It will not be much longer after the break, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since you indicated that the examination of this witness would take you one hour and a half, you have six minutes left to the one hour and a half. We adjourn until five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour asked me a question about the numbers that appear on the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can -- and the dates. The dates that appear on the photograph, I am informed, appear to be the date of the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor who took the photograph, and the number in brackets appears to be the sequence number of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, we left off your testimony in the village of Stanari, and you had told us about the separation into two groups, your group consisting of approximately 750 men. While you were at that location in the village of Stanari, were any provisions provided to you and to the other people who were in the trains? And when I say provisions, I mean was any food, water, any protective kind of garments, any sanitary facilities made available to you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, we did not receive anything. If anybody needed to go to the bathroom, they had to simply do it right there by the carriage. They did not provide us access to toilets or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I take it when you re-boarded the train, no additional amenities were provided to you.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. No, nothing was provided to us, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now if we could go to paragraph 43 of your evidence. In paragraph 43 of your evidence, Mr. Alic, you have described earlier the odyssey that took you to Omarska, then to Keraterm, and ultimately your return to Bosanski Novi. And you arrived in Bosanski Novi. You remained in the wagons, in the train cars, for two days, which is described in paragraph 43. My question, then, is: When you arrived at the -- when you arrived at the Mlakve stadium, you say: "They let us leave the wagons." Later on you say: "They took us to the stadium. They lined us up there and wrote down our names. They gave us one sardine can." And it goes on. My question is: Who are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I mean the Serbian troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the stadium itself, did you -- were you free to move around in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. We could only occupy one half of the stadium. We couldn't cross that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were you -- actually, let me show you the next exhibit, please, and it is an exhibit of a stadium at Mlakve and it has certain markings on it. I'm going to ask you about this exhibit after I get a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P82.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, did I show you a copy of a photograph yesterday, and did you show me where, in the stadium, guards took positions with guns, where there was a machine-gun post, where the changing rooms were located, and where the entrance to the changing rooms were located?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And does this photograph -- is this a photograph of the Mlakve stadium and the markings where you indicated those guns -- those positions were located?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, how far away from this stadium, Mr. Alic, was Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, behind this stadium, there is one auxiliary stadium. You know what approximately the width of that stadium could be. And then if you go on, you come across a river, and across that river is Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So from the stadium, you can see Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: You can. Right from here, on the right side, from the right angle of this picture, you can see some houses at the other end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you another exhibit, which I assume will be P83. Is that correct? Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. What is depicted, Mr. Alic, in Prosecutor's Exhibit P83?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: You see the stadium where we were detained. But we were only allowed to go halfway across the stadium, towards the railroad. We were not allowed to go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "stadium," Mr. Alic, are you referring to the football field that appears in the centre of this picture?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I mean. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you -- could you just briefly describe for us what the daily regimen was while you were at the Mlakve stadium. When did you get up in the morning? What did you do throughout the day? When were you fed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We didn't have our watches on or anything. We would get up in the morning. It would be misty usually, because there was a river nearby. Sometimes they would line us up and make us stand there in the sun. Sometimes they would make us eat grass or do other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you free to leave that stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. No way. The guards were all around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 44, you describe the incident where you lost your eye. Can you explain in more detail what happened and the circumstances under which you were struck.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I can describe it. One day they told us all of a sudden to go in quickly, and they pushed us with rifle butt. One of them hit me on my back. Another one grazed my eye, and I lost the sight in that eye. I couldn't see who it was who hit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before the break, I said there were six minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Almost done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You took already eight. Could you finish as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you in respect of the medical help: Was there medical help available at the Mlakve stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No way. What kind of medical help do you mean? There was not even food, let alone medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just direct Your Honours to paragraph 45, the last line in paragraph 45, the second word, which is "drug." Is, I'm told, should be "drag," from the Bosnian Serb version of the statement. I think that's an error. It should read: "We had to drag heavy rollers." But let me move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you the next exhibit, please. While this next exhibit is being prepared -- I'll just tell you what this exhibit is. It will arrive faster than I can tell you. Take a look at this exhibit, please. Do you recognise that exhibit, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges about this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I can. While I was at the camp, my sister was taking care of paperwork for me, because Serbs said whoever wants to leave Bosanski Novi will be released after some paperwork. My sister, Minka Mujic, did this because she was out there, free, and she brought these papers to the camp when she was finished but they still wouldn't release me. After that, they forced us to sign some papers they produced themselves in order to release us, papers saying that we were pledging all our property to Republika Srpska and that we are leaving Bosanski Novi of our own will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, what number would this exhibit have?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did your sister bring this document? What was the purpose of her going and getting this document?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: All of this was done so that I would be allowed to leave the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally, you indicate in paragraph 47 that: "Before we left the camp, they told us that if we wanted to leave, we had to sign a document that we were leaving Bosanski Novi municipality voluntarily, and they made us sign off our property." Again, who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Men came in uniforms, carrying these papers. Everything was already filled in. They only added our names, and we were only supposed to sign. It was said that we were leaving Bosanski Novi for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One final exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we really have to -- it was indicated one hour and a half. You've gone over it for some seven to eight minutes. The next exhibit would then get number P85, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, briefly tell the Judges what this exhibit is.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: This is my own certificate, saying that I spent four to five days in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I note, Mr. Alic, that the date that is referred to in this exhibit says from 9 June 1992 to 23 July 1992. You actually arrived in Bosanski Novi on 9 July and arrived in the camp on 11 -- I mean 9 June 1992 and arrived in the camp on 11 June 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm also counting the two days we spent in train cars. I'm counting from the day when we were expelled from our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, thank you very much for your examination and your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Is the Defence ready to start cross-examination of Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I indicated this morning prior to my completion of the cross-examination of the previous witness, Mr. Hasanovic, I've received some additional material this morning just before court that I haven't had the opportunity to review properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I take it that we can't finish the cross-examination of the witness anyhow before --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll not be able to finish the cross-examination anyhow, I take it, unless you say -- so you would have some extra time and then the witness would return this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. I think that what I was proposing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You indicated that the next witness would give his examination -- his testimony in chief first.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there was no -- there were some practical problems, perhaps. Have they been solved, Mr. Harmon? Mr. Tieger said that he would do everything to have the next witness available, but we have another problem. When we're talking about the next witness, I'd first have to go into private session for one moment, but not after having asked this witness to leave the courtroom just for a second. Mr. Alic, may I ask you just to follow the usher for one second. We have to discuss a procedural issue. But we'd rather do that in your absence. That's got nothing to do with yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Usher, could the witness remain standby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you will be examined by Defence counsel, but not at this very moment. I expect this to take place tomorrow. So you're free to go at this moment, but we'd like to see you back tomorrow. It's for all kind of practical reasons that we changed the order a little bit, and if it disturbs you, we apologise for that. Mr. Alic, may I instruct you not to speak with anyone, not with counsel, not with other people, not to discuss with them the testimony you have given until now and the testimony you are still about to give, presumably tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Alic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I did understand there are no protective measures whatsoever required for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct. And Your Honour, if I may briefly go into private session to raise one issue with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then return into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are then in open session again. Please proceed. Mr. Hannis, it's you who is going to examine the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Hidic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have one second left anyhow, I saw that in the statement of Mr. Alic, several times mjesna zajednica, or zajetnica [phoen] was mentioned of which I do not know what it means. It was not translated into English. Perhaps the interpreters could help us out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that means local commune.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Hidic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hidic. Please be seated. You'll be here with us this morning only for a limited, very limited period of time, but we'll continue this afternoon. So even if it's only 10 to 15 minutes at this moment, we'll continue later on. You'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to begin by having the witness shown his prior statements. We have three separate statements he made to the ICTY, including a supplement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in chronological order, the first one is in November 1999. There was a July 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the numbers for these exhibits would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The numbers would be P86 and P86.1; P87 and P87.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P86 would then be for the November 1999 statement, and P87 would be for the July of 2000 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And P88 will be for the 21st of May, 2003 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we should have also a supplement, or an addendum dated the 31st of July, 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Which would be P89.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, have you had a chance to review those prior statements of yours before coming into court today?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have any changes or additions you wanted to make to those statements prior to affirming to the Court that those are your true, full, and accurate statements in this matter?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to move the admission of these three statements and the supplement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They are admitted into evidence, in the absence of any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then at this time, Your Honour, before I ask the witness any questions concerning those, I would also like to have the Court consider some additional prior evidence of Mr. Hidic. First let me ask him a couple of questions regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, in addition to those written statements you provided to the OTP, have you testified here at the Tribunal in another matter in May of last year, in the Brdjanin case?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And yesterday and today, have you had a chance to review that prior testimony with the language assistant here at the OTP?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at this time, can you confirm to the Court that that prior testimony is your true, full, and accurate evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Your Honour, pursuant to Rule 92 bis (D) we would ask the court to consider that as also the evidence of Mr. Hidic in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now if we have time I'd like to read a brief summary of that evidence. I don't think it will take more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could then read it. Mr. Hidic, Mr. Hannis will now first read a summary of your statements, and then further questions will be put to you in that respect, but that will be only this afternoon. So I'd like you to listen carefully and try to remember for this afternoon what Mr. Hannis read to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, this witness is a Bosnian Muslim who lived in Bosanski Petrovac in 1992. In his evidence, he details the discriminatory and illegal treatment of non-Serbs in Bosanski Petrovac during that year. The witness provides evidence about SDS policies in Bosanski Petrovac, including the termination of non-Serbs from their employment, restrictions on their movement, and illegal detentions. He describes also the discriminatory nature of a disarmament campaign, which was directed solely at the non-Serb population in Bosanski Petrovac. After the deadline for surrender of weapons pursuant to that policy expired, all the Bosniak areas were surrounded and blocked, and the houses were searched. The witness will tell you there was no armed resistance by the Bosniak population at that time. Mr. Hidic also talks about the persistent state of fear among the Bosniak population in Bosanski Petrovac during 1992. He describes the detention facilities in the area, and he gives secondhand descriptions based on accounts provided to him by his relatives. He also recounts the destruction of non-Serb property and cultural monuments that occurred in Bosanski Petrovac during 1992. The witness further provides evidence about numerous killings in Bosanski Petrovac, and the lack of any punishment for the known perpetrators. He describes how non-Serbs had to exchange or surrender their real property before being allowed to leave the municipality. He recounts the mass expulsion of the Bosniak population from Bosanski Petrovac in late September 1992. In late 1995, the witness returned to Bosanski Petrovac, when the VRS had left the area. He discovered many original SDS documents in the municipal archives and he received others from other municipal employees. He has furnished those original documents to the OTP and he has identified and verified those documents in his prior statements and testimony before this Tribunal. Your Honour, his evidence is relevant to paragraphs 7, 19, 20 through 23 and 27, as well as counts 3, 7, and 8 of the consolidated indictment. That concludes my reading of his summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it's of any use to put the first questions to the witness at this moment, where we have to stop anyhow in a couple of minutes. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, after the witness is excused for this session, there's just a matter I'd like to correct on the record briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Hidic, you're excused for the moment. Usually I instruct witnesses not to speak with anyone about their testimony, but you've answered only one or two questions until now. We'd like to see you back at 3.30 in Courtroom II this afternoon. So if you'd now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we understood it was 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was some misunderstanding about the time of the Status Conference that would precede our hearing of this afternoon. We'd like, then, to see you back at 4.00 this afternoon in Courtroom II. Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, we can hear what you'd like to tell us in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what -- oh, no. It was -- no. I remember it was about the transcript, yes, correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was about a correction for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I just want to correct the record, in fact. Just on this question of whether the material is new or not new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I know that Mr. Harmon persists in the view that disclosure to the previous legal team is disclosure for all purposes. Now, Your Honour, with the greatest of respect to Mr. Harmon and his view, I do not. And I consider that continuing circular debates on this particular impasse between Prosecution and Defence are futile and arid and a waste of court time. And I want to place that on the court record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Mr. Harmon. You might not have heard me this morning, Mr. Harmon, when I said that since we'd like to use our time as efficiently as possible for this week, because it is -- we'd like to -- not to send witnesses home when they've not been examined. And I left it to the parties to address the matter in great detail in one week from now on. So if you'd like to -- well, just to oppose to what Ms. Loukas said, fine; but I don't want any long debate at this moment on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. We've had this debate many times. We can raise it with Your Honour tomorrow morning. We can raise it at any other time, but I think the issues have been addressed earlier and repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you disagree with Ms. Loukas. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There is just one further point, very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It refers to that question -- I'm sorry. Your Honour, my microphone again. Just one issue very briefly. It's in relation to an issue that Your Honour raised. Just in relation to that aspect of the cross-examination of the previous witness, Mr. Hasanovic, and I would direct Your Honours' attention to page 80 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The question I asked was: "Now, just going to events in Bratunac prior to the events you've spoken of today, were you aware of, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in approximately the 3rd of September, 1991, that there was shooting --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down because of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- Muslims towards the population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your headphones not on, you missed the -- could you please read it again and a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The point doesn't require much labouring, Your Honour. It's just that I indicated when Your Honour asked me the question that the -- your paraphrasing from the particular aspect of the transcript was perhaps not reflected in the transcript. And I just wanted to point out that page 80 is a little different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've taken that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's nothing -- Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There is. Mr. Harmon's problem: He comes into court and then we regard him as a fair target, Your Honour. No. What I'm about to say is a very mild thing. We were puzzled by Mr. Harmon inviting the court to go into private session a moment ago to mention the meeting tomorrow morning. Because the court had taken precisely the opposite view the other day, that it was important that the public should know that such meetings were taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon -- I think, as a matter of fact, since we do not know exactly why Mr. Harmon - perhaps I should have asked him - wanted to go into private session. You should have raised the issue in private session and if we would have agreed, we would have repeated it in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's -- Mr. Harmon, this Chamber has indicated in public that the Chamber had some involvement in meeting between the parties. That's public and for purposes we did not want to hide this for the public. Is there any -- okay. Then this matter has been settled as well. Then it's just -- it was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I say, the reason I raised it in open session is because I'm afraid is seemed simply blindingly obvious in the light of the court's attitude the other day that Mr. Harmon can't actually really have intended that this matter should be kept under wraps in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has been clarified now. There's no issue in that respect any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I mention one other point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but please keep in mind that we should have stopped five minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've offered the courtesy of the other counsel to say what they wanted to say. The fact that I'm just unlucky to be last should nevertheless allow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Say whatever you'd like to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's only this in relation to the meeting tomorrow morning is why I raise this, just so Your Honour knows, from a practical point of view, that we have prepared a batch of material. It is with -- it's not voluminous. It's with the Prosecution because we've had extensive discussions already in the course of this week. The Prosecution are invited to consider it. I hope it won't take very long because it represents some discussions already, so it's very close, I think, to an agreed batch of material anyway. And I would hope that we would be able to -- of course the Prosecution reserve their right on this because they haven't seen the final version, but I would hope that we would manage to get this to the Trial Chamber perhaps within the next hour, I don't know, so that you will have this material in preparation for the meeting tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm in this house anyway until 7.00 today, so whenever it's available to us, it's fine. We'll then -- but not after having thanked the interpreters and the technicians for the additional time. I wouldn't say they granted us, but we took from them. We'll adjourn until 4.00 this afternoon in Courtroom II. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.52 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I think there's no need to call the case because we're resuming the morning session. Or perhaps, just for certainty's sake, could you please call the case, the same one as this morning, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I never know whether this is a break or a new hearing. Just to summarise, the information I received is that the Prosecution will not call any more witnesses after Mr. Hidic this week, and the one remaining witness is cancelled?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do understand that he'll not be called at a later stage, but he'll not be called at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We do not intend to call him at all, at this point, Your Honour; whether the Court or Defence counsel wish to is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I also understand that the parties would agree if we would hear the testimony in chief this afternoon by Mr. Hidic, and that tomorrow Mr. Hidic and the other witness who is still waiting to be cross-examined would be cross-examined. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, including this witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be very helpful, and we feel confident of being able to finish tomorrow anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You know that was one of the major aims of this Chamber, not to send any witnesses home that should have to return at a later stage. Yes, Mr. Hannis.
