utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, and in the event that we happen to finish early tomorrow with some time unused, we are ready to perhaps read in some 92 bis summaries for witnesses from Brcko, Bratunac, Bosanski Novi, if the Court considers that a good way to use available courtroom time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it also depends on the Defence, but would you oppose against 92 bis, that is, 92 bis witnesses without cross-examination, I then take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, in the interest of the public trial concerns expressed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, in fact that's already been very kindly mentioned to us by the Prosecution and we indicated we have no objection whatsoever. It seems a perfectly sensible use of time if it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We might then hear some 92 bis evidence tomorrow without cross-examination. Mr. Hannis, then, please proceed. Mr. Hidic, there's a lot of practical discussions over your head, more or less. You'll now be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. You'll not be examined today by counsel for the Defence. That will take place tomorrow. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, welcome back. From your prior testimony in your witness statement, sir, I know there are some facts already in evidence. I would like to lead you briefly through those before I have some more detailed questions for you. But I understand, sir, that you are a Bosnian Muslim, or a Bosniak, who lived and worked in Bosanski Petrovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your employment before the war began in 1992, was as a skilled machine locksmith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what company did you work at or work for?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The name of the company was Bosnaplast, and it was located in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I also understand from your prior testimony that although you were not a member of the SDA in 1992, you currently are the president of the SDA in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Until last year; from 1999 until 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court if I'm correct when I say that the ethnic distribution of the population in Bosanski Petrovac in 1991 was approximately 3:1, or 75 per cent to about 25 per cent Serbs and Muslims? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: If you want me to give you a precise answer, according to the 1991 census, the correct ratio was 75:22.5 Serbs and Bosniaks; the remainder went to the so-called "others," which also comprised a number of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, how did the ethnic groups get along in Bosanski Petrovac before 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, what I can tell you is that up until that period of time, the relations in Bosanski Petrovac had been very good. People were tolerant and respectful of one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Beginning in 1992, did you notice a change in the relationships between or among the ethnic groups in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Obviously, with the changes that occurred at the time, which were the result of the multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the situation in Bosanski Petrovac changed as well. People were no longer as tolerant as before. However, the situation was still satisfactory, so to speak, up until the breakout of the war in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the multi-party elections and how that came out in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Concerning Bosanski Petrovac only, but also taking into account the larger situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia generally speaking, there was a lot of pre-electoral activity, a lot of campaigning in the municipality. We also started establishing political parties. That is, the political forces that would eventually take over power from the former regime in the former Yugoslavia. Work was done on the establishment of political parties in Bosanski Petrovac as well. The Serb population was more numerous, and they started with establishing political parties, which was also followed by a lot of campaigning which started in Bosanski Petrovac at that time. The Bosniak population followed suit, and so, generally speaking, there was a lot of activity which was geared towards the multi-party elections which were to take place very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were the results --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What were the results or the outcome of the elections in your municipality of Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: After the official elections in Bosanski Petrovac, the results concerning the local government, the local assembly, Municipal Assembly, were as follows: 50 to 33. So the SDS was represented with more than 60 per cent. Nine -- actually, eight seats went to the Party of Democratic Action. The remainder went to the former Reformists, that is, a movement for the reform of Yugoslavia. And a certain number of seats went to the SDP, the former Communists. But the majority of seats went to the representatives of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a result of those elections, how were the various offices in the municipality divided up? Can you tell us who was president of the municipality, who was head of the police department, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: After the results were declared officially and when implementation of the results started, there were a certain number of agreements that were reached by the political parties that had won the election. The SDS attempted to get most of the positions, and I think that they eventually did get most of the offices in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the president of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the president of the Municipal Assembly was and what his ethnicity was.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly was Rajko Novakovic, a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the head of the local police, his name and ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The head of the local police, that office was subject to a certain number of negotiations, because the Serb party insisted on having that office. I know that it was eventually Dragan Gacesa that got the post, who had, prior to that, worked in Bihac. So he was brought from Bihac to Bosanski Petrovac and appointed to the position of the head of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe from your prior testimony you indicated that there was some controversy about that position. Had the Muslims or the Bosniaks appointed a candidate for that position?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Bosniaks would have preferred the position of the commander of the police station in Bosanski Petrovac, so this was subject to a lot of discussions, and it was at one point promised to the Bosniak side that the office would go to them, which, however, was never implemented. There was no appointment of their candidate to the position of the chief of police, because the SDS did not want to yield them that particular office, which was coveted by the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After the elections and in early 1992, did you -- I think you indicated you began to see a change in the relations between the various ethnic groups, and particularly the Serbs and Muslims, or Bosniaks, in Petrovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. As time went by, as the new government was being established, a number of conflicts at the same time were breaking out elsewhere in Yugoslavia, first in Slovenia and then in Croatia, which was followed by the secession of Slovenia. So, obviously, the situation exacerbated in the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac, which, up until that time, had been a peaceful and tolerant milieu. So the overall events had an impact on what was going on in the Bosanski Petrovac municipality, where the situation was getting worse by the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you give us some examples of how the situation got worse? How did that manifest itself in everyday life for an average Bosniak or Muslim in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: What I can say is, for instance, that when it comes to the implementation of the election results and the distribution of posts amongst the parties, their initial agreement was not respected, and all offices, all positions, were kept by Serbs. The SDS managed to retain all key positions in Bosanski Petrovac. If that's what you had in mind concerning the setting up of the local government on the basis of the election results.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You indicated it seems that there was some pre-election agreement between the parties about distribution of post or positions?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There had been an agreement between the political parties that took part in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what that agreement was or what it called for?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I'm really not familiar with how they envisaged it, what they thought the executive government would be. As for the legislative power, I know that the president of the municipality was a Bosniak, a member of the SDA. This was Mr. Mustafa Ferizovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You indicated that the Serbs maintained most of the top positions in Petrovac, and you said the situation got worse. Were there certain restrictions or limitations placed on Muslims in the municipality beginning in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The events surrounding the election results took place in 1991. As for the beginning of 1992, the situation was already completely different. It was bordering on conflict, or a war. Actually, the war was going on in the immediate vicinity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in particular, the area of Bosanska Krajina. I'm referring to the events in Croatia. So this atmosphere of fear, of war psychosis, influenced the overall climate in the town itself, and the municipality also, generally speaking. And I'm referring both to the population and the political figures, people who were in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did this atmosphere of fear play out in the town? What were the things that happened to the local people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Specifically, as early as 1991, mobilisation started, or rather, voluntary engagement. Men went to war to Croatia. At the same time, the police reserve force was also mobilised. As for the economy, that area of life also experienced a lot of changes in terms of local leaders and managers. The production side experienced more difficulties. This was all reflected in the everyday life in our municipality. The general situation had an impact on the everyday life in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand that atmosphere had an effect on everyone in the municipality, but were there some effects that were different for Serbs and for non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am. And can you tell us what those were?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: At that time, a number of drastic changes occurred with respect to the relations between the communities at Bosanski Petrovac. There was a number of dismissals of Bosniaks, in particular after April and April events. So in April, May, and June, there were a lot of dismissals of Bosniaks. Shooting was also frequent, intimidation as well. A curfew was ordered by the police at that point in time, which, practically speaking, concerned only Bosniaks or Muslims and was applicable only to them on the -- in the area of the municipality. So the movement -- the freedom of movement was already limited. If you wanted to go to Sarajevo, for instance, or leave the territory of the municipality, you needed a special permit. True, we could still go to Bihac, but if you wanted to leave the area of the Bosanski Petrovac municipality, it was necessary to apply for a special permission. So it was during that period of time that, apart from the cases of intimidation, we saw the first killings, which added to the overall atmosphere of fear amongst Bosniaks in Bosanski Petrovac. Bosniaks hardly ever went out any more. They no longer moved so much around the town. Even in those neighbourhoods, in those areas where they were majority, because in those neighbourhoods as well, they were intimidated or provoked by various groups who would pass by, open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And around this time, was there any local programme about turning in weapons that affected Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It was publicly declared and publicly requested that Bosniaks turn in all personal weapons that they had, be it legally owned weapons that they may have had as hunters or on the basis of some other permit, but also illegal weapons, because some people were known to possess such weapons. The deadline was 20 or 30 days, I believe, by which the weapons had to be handed over to the police in Bosanski Petrovac. The local media, in particular, the local radio, broadcast this publicly. As for some people who were known to possess better quality weapons, they were visited by individuals of Serb ethnicity or by employees of the police or members of the army, who would take over their weapons, especially when they were known to possess good-quality hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this call for surrender of weapons became publicly announced?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that on the 27th or 28th - I cannot recall the exact day - the entire town, the centre of the town of Bosanski Petrovac, was blocked by the army. Several transporters or personnel carriers participated in this operation, which focused on those streets and those areas where Bosniaks lived. The purpose of this operation was to search for weapons. I personally witnessed one such operation in two or three houses on the street where I lived. Unfortunately, those who were carrying out the searches did not find anything. I don't know whether they had picked those locations on their free will or if they had any orders to that effect, but they entered into maybe 20 or 30 houses, and I am referring to the area of town where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you a couple of questions about that answer. First you said it was the 27th or the 28th. Can you tell us what month and what year?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in May, 1992, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I read in the English transcript where you say you personally witnessed one such operation in two or three houses, and then you said: "Unfortunately, those who were carrying out the searches did not find anything." If you've said "unfortunately," can you explain why you thought that was unfortunate that they didn't find anything.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know why. I just happened to use that expression. I really don't know why I used that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, did your house get searched during this operation or a similar operation?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know by whose authority or where this call for weapons to be surrendered came from? You said it was announced on the radio, I believe, but can you tell us by whose authority. Was it police? Was it some municipal body?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think it came from the top municipal authorities, who at the time functioned as semi-military authorities. They must have issued an order to that effect, which was then transmitted to the police station in Bosanski Petrovac, and that was how this search and seizure of weapons from the Muslim community was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know from your statements and your testimony that you're familiar with the term "Crisis Staff," but in May of 1992, did you know of that term and whether there was such a body in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who the members of the Crisis Staff were in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I know some of them. I knew who they were at the time as well, by virtue of their official capacity, those who were members of the civilian government. The president of the Crisis Staff was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Petrovac, that is, Mr. Novakovic. Then, in terms of hierarchy, it was the president of the Executive Board; the secretaries of the Municipal Assembly as well; the assistants, or heads as they were called at the time, of various departments; the head of the police station; and also representatives of the then-legal and legitimate army. Because a certain number of JNA personnel had remained in Bosanski Petrovac who attended those meetings, meetings of the Crisis Staff, by virtue of their membership in those army units, together with the representatives of the civilian part of the armed forces, that is, the Territorial Defence, or whatever it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the members of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: By and large, the members of the Crisis Staff were Serbs, and the representatives of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, I want to jump ahead for a minute, because I want to show you some documents, and in order to do that, I need to go into the future a little bit. I know there came a time where you were expelled from Petrovac, but then you came back in September of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was your purpose for returning at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Of course, on the 14th of September, Bosanski Petrovac was free. Since I was in Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout the war, I was in Central Bosnia, living in Zenica at the time, I travelled during four or five days in a roundabout way through Glina and Bihac to Bosanski Petrovac, because it was a free town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say it was a free town, did you mean this Serb army had left the area, the VRS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. When I arrived, I didn't see a single Serb soldier in Bosanski Petrovac, because they had all left. They left Bosanski Petrovac on the 14th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on that occasion in 1995 and shortly thereafter, and on into 1996, did you come across certain original documents of the Crisis Staff and other municipal authorities still in the archives and municipal buildings in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: First of all, or rather, at first, I didn't pay any attention to documents which remained in Bosanski Petrovac, in the city authorities or in municipal authorities. I had to go back to Zenica a few days later, because I had the task to organise the return of Bosniaks who had left Bosanski Petrovac and needed to return home. It took me a month, travelling around Central Bosnia, to rally Bosniaks and to appeal to them to return to their homes in Bosanski Petrovac. In late October/beginning of November, I returned, and when I came to the town hall, I noticed a lot of documentation simply scattered around and lying on the ground in corridors, because the army had simply stampeded through the building, leaving a mess behind them. And we needed to put these things in order and return the documentation to archives. In this way, I got hold of certain documents that I found scattered everywhere around the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand that you received documents from other municipal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. employees and eventually you turned over those documents to the OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: True. I asked everyone not to throw away these papers, and people understood that they needed to be preserved. From that point on, they started bringing me these papers, and I filed them carefully, with the idea that they needed to be kept, that maybe later they will have their purpose. And in this way, I managed to preserve a lot of evidence that could be saved, of course, of the times in which we lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, in May of last year, you testified in the Brdjanin case and identified and spoke about a number of those documents here in this building; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have binders with approximately 45 documents that I would like to show the witness and I would like to tender at this time. I actually only intend to ask him about four of those documents. But if we could pass around those binders, I would like to then discuss at least four of those documents with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the benefit of counsel and the Court, Your Honour, all of these documents were items that were shown to Mr. Hidic during his trial testimony in the Brdjanin case, and pursuant to Rule 92 bis (D) and our procedure in this Court, I would like to make an oral application at this time that these documents be admitted by the Court in connection with that prior testimony that has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we'd first give a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P90 for the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the binder. And then, Madam Registrar, since in the binder we find 45 tabs, that each of these documents would then be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it just gets one number, but if we refer to it, we refer to the tab in which we find the specific documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, in that binder, you'll see the little tabs on the right-hand side with the number, and the first document I want to ask you about I believe is at tab 34. If you could go to the number 34 and look at the document behind that tab. There should be both an English and a B/C/S version of the same document. Can you tell me what that document is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me what that document is in your binder, please, behind tab 34. At the top, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Serbian Republic, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Municipal Assembly of Petrovac, Crisis Staff, number 57-92. If you mean the left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's the same document I'm talking about, and this appears to be the minutes of the 35th Session of the Petrovac municipality Crisis Staff. And could you go down to where it says "agenda," and item number 1 on the agenda. Could you read out what that says.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: "Consideration of the situation and measures to remove the consequences of combat operations, or war operations." That is one item.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't see any agenda here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It appears that the agenda was adopted unanimously. And the paragraph following that that starts "The president gave a brief description..." would you read that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: "The president gave a brief description of the situation on the front line, indicating that our losses were two dead, 19 wounded, adding that the Crisis Staff is expected to take a clear stance vis-a-vis the Muslims. And military post 4552 demands that measures be taken to enable them to act in an operative way and carry out activities in the rear of our forces." Shall I go on? "Dragan Gacesa emphasises that there is a list, including 40 or so persons, who are believed to be organised as a separate group or have come out with extremist, fundamentalist Islamist positions. Most of them are fugitives and unavailable for questioning by the authorities. Most of them belong to various citizen groups. The list includes the names of people who have been found to possess illegal weapons. One possible solution would be to isolate a number of such dangerous persons at the police station, and the second measure could be to isolate extremists, but outside of Petrovac." Do you think it's necessary for me to go on reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The next paragraph below that I think indicates that the view prevailed that isolation of the extremists outside Petrovac would be dangerous to those people, so it was best to isolate them in a well-guarded facility on the outskirts of town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And underneath, there's a heading entitled "Decision" in English. Do you see that in your B/C/S copy?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it indicates that individuals who possess illegal weapons or who have been registered as Muslim extremists shall be detained and held in custody?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- I've got a slight difficulty in that I've got my gown trapped in my chair, so I can hardly stand up, but leaving that aside, may I -- I can't do it. May I take it off, Your Honour? Because it's quite ridiculous. I can't stand up straight with my gown in my -- may I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try and see if I can avoid that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've taken off your wig already, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That is as far as I'm going, Your Honour. My question, getting back to serious matters, is that I'm wondering where this is going, because we've had two or three questions now and this witness has read passages from a meeting at which he was not present, and I've been waiting to see whether it is leading to some question along the lines of his being able to offer something of his own knowledge that's in some way connected with this. Because if all he is doing is telling us what the minutes of this meeting say, it isn't really evidence from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If my learned friend will be patient for another minute or two, I do have some questions to ask the witness regarding what we're reading out right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed. We have to wait and see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Hidic, it indicates that a certain house will be set up as a detention facility. Are you aware of any detention facilities that were established in Petrovac on or about this time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time. But a month later, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was that facility, and what was it called?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It was called Kozila workers' labour site. Unfortunately, that facility was adjusted to become a camp, detaining about 50 to 60 Bosniaks from Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, before we continue, could I just seek to clarify something, perhaps together with the witness. On the first page of this document, you read a part where VP-4552 is mentioned. Could you please read that part again in your own language, or tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just this part: "Military post box 4552." VP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue the next lines as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to indicate that they do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Requests that measures be taken to disable their operative action and activities in the rear or behind the lines of our forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it is translated as to disable them. In the earlier translation, we saw, and I referred to page 16, line 19, to enable them. There seems to be a slight mistake. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned the disarming operation that was going on in Petrovac before. Were there certain Muslims or Bosniaks in town who had been detained as a consequence of what was happening with that disarming operation?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe there were people who were taken into custody and people who were detained, but at the police station, not at the camp. They were detained at the police station, while the activity of collecting weapons was still under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I would like to go to another document. Mr. Hidic, it's behind tab 33, the one immediately in front of the one that you're looking at. And can you tell me if what you have is dated the 30th of June and is the minutes of the 41st Session of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Beneath my English portion where it says "Agenda," and item number 1 is "Political and security situation in Petrovac municipality"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The second full paragraph after that says: "He relayed requests from soldiers he had talked to for a more radical attitude toward the Muslims of Petrovac." And "he" appears to be referring to Rajko Novakovic, whose name appears in the paragraph immediately above. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Give me just a minute, please. You mean paragraph 2, if I'm looking at the right thing. Yes. This is a reflection of what Rajko Novakovic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. And if you could go to the third sentence after that one I just read, and it begins "The Muslims of Petrovac are behaving as if they're wounded..." could you read that for us, please, and the following sentence.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: "Muslims in Petrovac are like a wounded beast in great terror, great fear. A certain number of them have yet to be arrested, out of caution, and later introduce the work obligation, because there will be a lot of work involved in harvest season. I insist that a certain number of motorised saws be commandeered as part of this labour work obligation and placed at the disposal of the brigade."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters repeat that these things are difficult to interpret off the cuff without the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It would have been easier if the interpreters would have been provided with an existing B/C/S copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I will make sure that is done differently the next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And although I see that there is some slight difference, it appears to be substantially the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, if you could go, then, to the heading that's called "Conclusions" and read out number 1 for us. And then I'll have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: "Until the prisons in Kozila are put in operation, organise the arrest and neutralisation of everybody who is suspected to be a danger to Serbs." If necessary, I can repeat: "Until the prisons, or the prison in Kozila, is put in operation, make a plan to arrest and take into custody all able-bodied Muslims who are suspected of potentially doing any harm to Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Dragan Gacesa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you would stop there, please, and let me ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I wonder if I might make a suggestion. It seems -- we've got a rather unsatisfactory situation. The witness is being asked to read a document in his own language, which has already been translated and which we have in these bundles in English. And they've presumably been translated -- I'm not in a position to judge the translations, but they've been translated presumably under more favourable circumstances than the interpreters face today because those original translators at least had the advantage of having a document in front of them. So what's happening is by asking the witness to read the Serbian version we're ending up with what I think today's interpreters would acknowledge to be, I won't say inferior but a translation in more difficult circumstances, so a rather rougher translation, which is not helpful at all. It would be -- again, no disrespect to the interpreters saying "not helpful at all," because it's not helpful that we end up with two translations. Wouldn't it be more satisfactory if counsel, if he wants to refer to these particular passages, were to read the English translation so -- identifying the passage, so the witness can follow it in the original language, and then the questions, which after all presumably is the point of all this anyway, whatever questions follow then from the reading of this text can follow. But we'll avoid this complete mess of the public transcript having the unsatisfactory translation given under difficult circumstances by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's indicated already by Mr. Hannis that next time we'll do it in a different way, such as that the interpreters will have the translation available and are able to check on the reading of the witness whether the translation is satisfactory. Under the present circumstances, I would say that since we now get, although perhaps a translation which is made on the spot, without any time for reflection on details, that at least we are able to satisfy ourselves that the translation as we receive it now, although not exactly the same, is in line with the translation we have on paper. I do not mind if you would, in cross-examining the witness, you would refer to the translation as it appears in English on paper. To ask Mr. Hannis to read it in English would, in my view, not be the most favourable solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that -- Your Honour has in a sense anticipated my next point, but I don't quite see what difficulty there would be in switching to that technique now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection. I was only concerned about my sore throat that I've been fighting all week, but we only have two more documents to go and I'll be happy to read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's finish as we did it now, and let's -- if the witness reads slowly, then I think we -- at least I find it very satisfactory to see that even the translation that's made on the spot reflects, I would say for 98 per cent, what is on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if there would be an extra copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do have an extra copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll provide an extra copy at this moment to the English booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That earlier sentence you read about the Muslims of Petrovac behaving as if wounded and showing great fear, is that an accurate reflection of the mood in the town as you told us about earlier?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Of course. You see that they themselves note that, the representatives of authorities in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at this time, in June, did there appear to be an increasing number of detentions of Muslim or Bosniak men in Petrovac town?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I have already said which number of detainees we were talking about, men who were taken into custody and detained in the Kozara camp when it was put into operation. And in June, there were only preparations in the run-up to this period when they would be taken into custody and detained. In the meantime, a certain number of them were already in prison, and the prison close to the police station in Bosanski Petrovac was too small to take in everybody who was taken into custody, and probably for that reason they were thinking of providing a larger facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what the capacity of the police station detention facility was?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I know that those were basements, but you have to take my word for it if I say that I've never been there. I don't know what they were like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think we can describe that as fortunate. I will take your word for it. Can you tell me now -- if you can set that document aside. If you can go to tab 39 in the binder and look at that document. And I believe, sir, that should be an August 3rd, 1992 record of the 45th meeting of the commission. I'm not clear what commission it is, but it's in Petrovac. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I see it's the conclusion after item 1. But I wouldn't know at this point ... I think that the commission in question here had been tasked with gathering information on the exchange of population, as they commonly referred to it in the area of Bosanski Petrovac, but it was actually departures from the area. So a commission of that kind I know was established at one point, and they were in charge of gathering information relating to all those departures of the citizens of Bosanski Petrovac from the area of the municipality. The information concerned also data on their property. If I'm reading it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: But with your permission, please. Here, the commission worked only on the exchanges between Bosanski Petrovac and Bihac, both ways. So they must have been working according to that kind of task or order. The people in question, I think, are Bosniaks who were supposed to leave to Bihac for the purpose of being reunited with their family, as it was called at the time. Apparently, members of their families had left for Bihac before this period of time and were now in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And let me ask you a couple of questions. At the top it indicates who is present, and among those names are Rajko Novakovic and Gacesa, Dragan Gacesa. And as I understood you told us before, that's the president of the Crisis Staff and the chief of police; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. And also Latinovic, Bogdan, who was the president of the Executive Board, the second in power, as a president of an executive municipal body. Dragan Milanovic, a deputy to the Assembly. Milan Vidovic, who was here by virtue of his capacity as the head of the hospital. Obrad Vrzina, a military man. Jovica Sepa for the military issues and for economics issues, and Drago Korda, who was there as a representative of the Red Cross organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see two names below that. Can you tell us who those individuals are, in the next line.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Zare Sikman was the secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Petrovac. As for Slobodan Brcin, he must have been invited to attend because he was a lawyer. So they probably wanted some kind of legal advice from him, or he was there in some other capacity. I'm not sure exactly in which capacity he attended this meeting. Personally, I know that he's a lawyer, so most probably it was because of that that he was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, and I see that the agenda item number 2 was to examine the security situation and the question of Muslims. And in the discussion about agenda item 2 that appears below, it indicates that there were a number of Muslim citizens who attended the meeting and asked questions, including whether Muslims in Petrovac could be guaranteed their safety. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They're talking about a group of Muslim citizens of Bosanski Petrovac who had requested to be able to attend this session of the Crisis Staff, and also to be able to present their opinion or their requests from the municipal authority of Bosanski Petrovac. The request in question, in my opinion, must have been to leave the area, to move out from the area of Bosanski Petrovac. This is a rather loose forum of citizens. They refer to themselves as forum of citizens of Bosanski Petrovac. And because it was impossible to reach any agreement whatsoever with this regard, they must have tried to talk about the issue with the top municipal leaders and try to find some solution for the movement of the population. Because the situation had become critical for the Muslim community.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it appears this commission reached a resolution regarding the moving out of Muslim people, and it was going to be the one to decide who can leave, and the condition for leaving was that people had to either exchange or give up all of their property to the state, that is, to the Serbian Municipality of Petrovac. Do you see that, and is that consistent with your knowledge of what happened in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't even have to look at it, because I know that what followed was an increase of interest amongst Muslims of Bosanski Petrovac, and they had to fill out some forms at the land survey department. They had to also pay all the taxes, all the arrears that they had to pay for their land so that they could obtain some sort of permission which would enable them to go to the police and request formally to be enabled to leave the area. This piece of paper would have proved that they no longer had any obligations with respect the municipality, that all the bills had been paid, and so on and so forth. A large number of citizens accepted this, and soon a huge line, a huge queue of citizens could be seen at the town hall, people who came there as a result of these discussions, with the purpose of obtaining the necessary documents to leave the Bosanski Petrovac municipality. It was there that they were issued certificates whereby they were leaving their property, they were giving up their property and leaving it to the municipal authorities of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did they receive any compensation for their property that they were giving up in order to leave, any reimbursement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: If you understood me correctly, they had to pay taxes. They had to pay their electricity and water bills so that they could eventually get the final certificate, which was issued by the police and which then enabled them to move out from the Bosanski Petrovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if I personally owned any real property, my house or the land it was on, or a business, did I get any reimbursement from the city in exchange for turning it over to them, if I had to do that in order to leave?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Purportedly, it was done on a voluntary basis. They were leaving their property of their own will to the Serbian municipal authorities of Bosanski Petrovac. With your permission, if I may add, I have personal knowledge of that because I myself had to sign a paper of that kind. I think I still have it somewhere, their certificate which contains all the information about my family, members of my family, of my household, and which proves that I had no obligations with respect the municipal authorities. On the basis of that paper, I was issued a certificate by the police, which certificate was supposed to enable me to leave the Bosanski Petrovac municipality. But this, however, never took place, was never implemented, until the time of my eviction, that is, the 24th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And did you leave voluntarily? Would you classify your departure as voluntary?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It was treated as having been done on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But it sounds like you don't consider it voluntary. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean, who on earth would leave his or her property just like that, without any compensation, without even a thank-you note? Also, we were sent away with shots. Shots were heard as we were leaving. You cannot talk about any generous giving up of one's property while at the same time being forced to leave the town where they had lived, where they were born, and the property to which they were legally, of course, entitled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And how many people left? How many Muslims or Bosniaks left Petrovac by the time you left in September? If you know.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe their number was somewhere around 2.600 or 2.700 of Bosniaks who left in the last batch. There had been a prior departure as well, two busloads, I think, in the direction of Bihac, but the number was maybe 100 or 150 persons. The largest number of Bosniaks were evicted on the 24th of September, and the number in question is anywhere between 2.500 and 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And of the total population of Bosniaks or Muslims in Petrovac prior to the start of the war, what percentage would that be that left during that time? If you know.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that a very small number of people left Bosanski Petrovac. Those who did, left for Bihac. Maybe 50 people or so, maybe even less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one more document I want to ask him about. I think I can finish it in about five more minutes. I'm not sure when you were going to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that after these five minutes we'll adjourn for the day, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you would set that aside and look at one last document for me, which is behind tab number 30. And it's a report on the events in Bosanski Petrovac from June 1992 until the departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I have a question for the interpreters, because my English translation, at the top, refers to the Bosanski Petrovac Country Club, although I'm told perhaps a better translation would be the Bosanski Petrovac Expatriates' Club.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, that English translation then should be corrected, and "Country Club" will be changed to "Expatriates' Club" and I will provide a corrected copy to the Court tomorrow, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see that document, Mr. Hidic? Do you know what that document is?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about the Expatriates' Club of Bosniaks from Bosanski Petrovac who, having been evicted from Bosanski Petrovac, arrived here and found themselves in Zagreb. A large number of Bosniaks ended up in Zagreb. And by establishing this club, they tried to maintain some sort of link with the people from the area, also with the people from the area who used to be seasonal workers in West European countries. But it's a club established by evicted Bosniaks. And the natives of Petrovac who lived in Zagreb, because a certain number of Bosniaks from Petrovac used to live in Zagreb, and still do, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this appears to be a chronology of the events, particularly events of a discriminatory nature against Muslims or Bosniaks in Petrovac from June through September of 1992. Have you seen it before, and are you familiar with where this information came from to go into this report?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I first came across this information after the war, that is, three years later. And upon returning to Bosanski Petrovac, when some -- one of the people who had been in Zagreb showed me this document. On the basis of this and the statements of the Bosniaks who had been evicted from Petrovac, I was able to establish that this is a true review of the events in and surrounding Bosanski Petrovac between April and the 24th of September, the day of the eviction from Bosanski Petrovac. Also, I have in mind statements that I heard elsewhere and articles published in the media, as they were appearing at the time, in Bosnia and out of Bosnia. The information is almost identical when it comes to the contemporaneous situation in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes my direct examination. I would like to tender the binder and the 45 documents contained therein at this time, as I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, the documents are admitted into evidence. When a new translation is made where the "Country Club" is replaced, please draw the attention to those preparing this new translation that it's not only in the top of the document that the "Country Club" appears, but also in the few last pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. We'll change every reference to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going to say, we have prepared -- we have three copies of material for tomorrow morning's meeting. Shall I hand them in to Ms. Philpott after Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last message I got just before entering into this courtroom is that the parties would prefer to meet even today, and since we are not sitting until 7.00, I indicated that I would be available until 7.00. That would be for approximately one hour. So I leave it up to the parties whether they prefer to meet now or tomorrow morning at 7.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I spoke with Mr. Harmon and Mr. Tieger about this possibility, they indicated at that time that they would be available, if that was agreeable with the Court. I don't know if they're watching right now, but I will try to contact them immediately. Where should we meet?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would also certainly prefer, thank you, to meet this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that would be in my chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would that be in about -- I've got to find Ms. Loukas. She is not far away, Your Honour. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you'll find her within ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ten or 15 minutes, I think, Your Honour, yes. As soon as we can make a phone call, we can find her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although my time today, but the same would be true tomorrow, is limited to approximately one hour on from 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. We understand. No. We know. She is very close by, Your Honour. So we can't guarantee ten minutes, but it would be very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn, but not after having instructed you, Mr. Hidic, not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given and you're still about to give tomorrow, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, where we'll resume at 9.00 in Courtroom I, if I'm not mistaken, Madam Registrar. So we'd like to see you tomorrow. You'll then be examined by counsel for the Defence, and perhaps by the Judges as well. Yes? Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Shall I just hand these to Your Honour now? These are for the meeting we're about to have. The sooner Your Honour has them, the better --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- I'd suggest. There are three copies there, Your Honour, for Your Honour's colleagues as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As you know, the involvement of the Chamber is limited to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand that, but it seemed appropriate that Your Honour's fellow Judges should have the same material anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll make sure that this happens. We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of April 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.52 p.m.
